News.title: Man admits drugging and raping wife over 20 years
News.content:
A man accused of drugging and raping his wife without her knowledge over a 20-year period has admitted 60 offences against her.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's legal right to anonymity, had already admitted some counts at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court, including rape.

The wife watched proceedings from the public gallery supported by members of her family.

The husband, in his sixties, became visibly emotional as he repeated the word guilty to dozens of charges - including multiple counts of rape, assault by penetration and administering a substance with intent - and at one point was invited to sit down in the dock by the judge.

Twelve other men deny multiple serious sexual offences against the same woman.

The husband, from the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, will be sentenced for the counts he has admitted at the conclusion of the trial.

A 13th man previously admitted sexual offences against the woman.

The husband's offending against his wife, who he was married to for decades, took place over a period going back to 2004, while the accusations involving the other men range from September 2018 to November 2025.

The other defendants are:

Philip Wild, 58, from Stockport

Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport

Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester

Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester

Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport

Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport

Mohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abode

Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich, Cheshire

Richard Townsend, 37, from Rochdale

Karl Lindsay, 55, Taunton, Somerset

Daniel Rayner, 42, from, Whitstable, Kent

David Graves, 59, from, Ilkeston, Derbyshire

The trial is due to continue in the coming weeks.

News.title: AI 'kill switch' may need to be mandatory, Anthropic co-founder tells BBC
News.content:
Clark told the BBC that specifics around "kill switch" requirements and verification should be part of "the larger policy conversation" taking place around AI.

"Should you mandate for companies to definitely have a kill switch? Is that kill switch verifiable by a third party?" he asked.

"I think that's the kind of thing society is going to want to know and might want to eventually pass rules around."

Anthropic, which was formed in 2021 by a group of former employees of its rival OpenAI, is currently at the centre of a debate around AI safety.

Last week, a post from an artificial intelligence researcher who quit Anthropic over concerns AI could wipe out humanity went viral.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger said he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was ">10% within the next decade".

Computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC on Friday that a 10% chance of AI killing all humans was "not unreasonable", external.

He and others with similar concerns have suggested AI could do so by taking control of important systems connected to the internet and turning them on humans.

However, some in the AI industry have suggested the fears around it destroying humanity are overstated or may be designed to generate hype.

Clement Delangue, leader of the developer platform Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI bots, said last week: "Sorry, but asking Jacob [Coxon] about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change."

"Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."

George Arison, the leader of Grindr, said the fears going around AI tools were being used by the companies to support their business plans.

Anthropic, which was valued at $965bn (Â£713bn), is preparing for an initial public offering on the stock market, allowing people to buy shares in its firm.

OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn (Â£630bn), had been expected to do the same, but OpenAI's Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year due to the current debate around AI safety.

Arison said: "The only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"

Asked what percentage he would put on all humans being killed by AI, Clark said: "I don't think these statistics are that useful", but added that allowing AI to continue as a "totally unregulated industry" was a bad idea.

"We are rolling dice with immense risks," Clark said. "And the point is, we have to change the course of this industry."

News.title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet
News.content:
The Â£72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers from two British billionaires is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.

In short, how should political parties be paid for, and by who?

And, what is a legitimate donation and what isn't?

It is worth setting out the law, in broad terms, now and how the government hopes to change it.

Right now, there is no limit on how much anyone, living in the UK or abroad, can give to a British political party as long as the individual is registered to vote in the UK.

But the government has been planning a change in the law for months, which would limit donations from Brits abroad to Â£100,000 each per year, backdated to 25 March this year.

But, crucially, the law hasn't changed yet and some of the key details in that proposed new law - such as what residency requirements would need to be passed to be classified as no longer being abroad - haven't been decided yet.

The reason for that date, 25 March, ministers argue, is that is the day a review by the retired civil servant Philip Rycroft was published,, external the first recommendation of which was that there should be "an annual cap on political donations from British voters living abroad".

On that same day, the then-cabinet minister Steve Reed told the Commons, external that cap would be Â£100,000 per year. He also added that it would "apply retrospectively" from that date onwards, even though the law at the time, and indeed now, has not yet changed.

Two big questions arise from this plan: is it proportionate to limit what British folk abroad can donate to UK political parties, given they are arguably less invested in the country than people living here?

And is it unfair, even morally questionable, to pass a law, but then backdate when its impact begins?

Fast forward to the last few days and along come these colossal donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires who until recently lived in Hong Kong and Thailand respectively.

They have both now returned to the UK.

In his first interview since these donations became public, Nigel Farage told me unequivocally that the money from both men was legal under the law as it stands now.

But he was equivocal when I asked him if they would legal under the law the government hopes to pass shortly.

"Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever," Farage told me.

Ah, today, I pointed out.

"Retrospectively declaring donations illegal - that simply cannot be," he pressed on, adding "you cannot confiscate money that has been given legally within the law as it stands."

That is a political, perhaps moral argument, but not a legal one - if the government changes the law, the law of the land will have changed, possibly with consequences for whether those donations are legal.

News.title: Nato jets down drone that entered Lithuanian airspace
News.content:
Nato fighter pilots have shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace overnight, the Lithuanian president said.

Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.

Lithuanian President Gitanas NausÄda wrote in a statement on X: "A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets."

The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, a spokesperson for the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said.

Drone alerts sounded across the capital Vilnius and surrounding region earlier on Tuesday.

Lithuania's armed forces and Italian pilots serving in the Nato Air Defence Mission "showed a swift and responsible response" to the drone incursion, Lithuania's Ministry of Defence said.

NausÄda's post on social media added: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."

Moscow has not commented on the incident.

Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.

Drone sightings were reported in Lithuania on Sunday. The crisis management centre later said an object had "likely" entered from Belarus and travelled across the country's territory before entering the airspace of Russia. The 13 September incident did not trigger air threat alerts.

Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.

Residents in Lithuania's capital were forced to take shelter across Vilnius in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.

Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.

Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.

Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".

News.title: Burnham cancels engagements after death of his father
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cancelled official engagements on Monday and Tuesday following the death of his father Roy, who had Alzheimer's.

He had been due to host a meeting of business leaders in Downing Street on Monday, and was expected to speak at the annual trade union TUC Congress in Brighton on Tuesday.

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

He had also said his father's illness was so advanced that he did not know his son had become prime minister.

Burnham told the BBC that while his father could not be there when he entered No 10 to take up the role, he and his mother had "exchanged a few words about my dad and how proud he would be".

"That's a little hard, but then again I've said, it's their achievement", he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg in July.

"The emotion of that moment was, well, bittersweet - it was painful in one way but beautiful in another."

The prime minister later said care home staff had shown his father footage of him entering Downing Street, calling it a "wonderful" thing.

Burnham said he wanted to help "my dad and the millions like him" when setting out plans to reform adult social care.

He said he had been "overwhelmed" by the skills and professionalism of care workers supporting his father.

Burnham has described how his father, a former telephone engineer, had raised him with "laughter, love and support" alongside his mother Eileen in Culcheth, Cheshire.

In his 2024 book Look North, he wrote that neither of his parents had attended university, but could have done had they "grown up in a different time and different place".

"Their knowledge of that fact seemed to make them all the more determined that their three sons would go."

Opposition politicians have offered their condolences to Burnham and his family.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "No matter how old you are, or how much you try to prepare, losing your father is a profoundly painful experience.

"A part of your life that has always been there is suddenly gone forever and it can feel as though a part of you won't ever be the same again."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "My heart goes out to the prime minister on the loss of his dad.

"From our conversations he sounded like a wonderful man."

Green party leader Zack Polanski said: "There are moments in life such as this sad time that transcend politics and I join the whole country in sending condolences."

News.title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour after 'Free Palestine' speech
News.content:
Rapper Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran's US tour after making pro-Palestinian comments on stage earlier this month.

The artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - had been the opening act for Sheeran's Loop tour, but was criticised by Jewish groups after saying "Free Palestine" at two concerts and making political speeches.

Macklemore stood by his comments on Monday, confirming that he had been cut from the tour and writing in a statement that the real victims are the Palestinian people in Gaza.

Ed Sheeran has not yet commented, and who will replace Macklemore for the rest of the tour is unknown.

The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore, a long-time pro-Palestine activist, performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."

He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.

After that performance, the campaign group StopAntisemitism criticised the rapper, saying "Jewish fans bought tickets to see Ed Sheeran sing... not to be ambushed by Macklemore's anti-Israel propaganda."

The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience.

"Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.

Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

News.title: Staff slept while patient killed at NHS mental health unit
News.content:
Hugo's father, William Flint Cahan, who has attended each day of the inquest with other family members, says there was "complacency" by staff, as well as a lack of care.

He maintains his son's death was "preventable had the level of care been as it should have been."

Hugo's brother, Jolyon, who is an NHS doctor, says the "litany of failures, both incompetence and dishonesty, that pervaded the care of both patients was harrowing."

Over the past 12 years, local coroners have sent at least 29 Prevention of Future Deaths (PFD) notices to the Trust. These are sent to an organisation when a coroner identifies problems which, if not dealt with, could lead to further deaths.

The BBC has analysed the reports which cover both in patient and community services. In more than half of cases there had been a failure to properly assess the risk the patient posed to themself or to others. Poor communications between staff, other agencies and families were also repeatedly highlightedy.

The strongest warnings were about poorly carried out observations and falsified records â basic care needed to keep patients safe.

A report in 2021 by the coroner that carried out the Flint Cahan inquest warned that "a culture of impunity existed" at the Trust where "inaccurate and misleading recording of clinical records was tolerated."

In 2024, two further reports highlighted observations being missed then records falsified to suggest patients had been checked.

In response to one of the PFD's, the Trust said extensive training programmes and quality checks were introduced.

In 2025, a fourth report, into the death of a young woman, again highlighted falsified observation records. The coroner said, "despite assurances" from the Trust in numerous action plans", the inquest had "revealed widespread concerns" about how observations were carried out across two wards."

Other serious concerns raised in the reports include, how staff have responded to emergencies, with delays in resuscitation and - on one occasion - nursing staff giving chest compressions to a patient's stomach rather than their chest.

Brian Dow of the mental health charity, Rethink, is calling for a national register of patient safety to keep tabs on the type of care mental health units across the country are providing.

"We have been here before" with poor observations, records being falsified and unacceptable care, he says.

"We have got to have a better approach to patient safety in what are the most difficult and most vulnerable wards with the people who are the most unwell."

In a statement, Dr David Bridle, Chief Medical Officer at ELFT, said the Trust is deeply sorry to Hugo's family for the failings in his care.

He said the actions of the staff identified by the coroner were "wholly unacceptable and do not reflect the standards, values or behaviours we expect".

Dr Bridle says the Trust has worked to improve its services and "will ensure the learning from the coroner's findings informs our continuing work to strengthen patient safety and care."

News.title: Harry and Meghan to have security review and children change school
News.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are going to be given a review of their publicly-funded security after their return to live in the UK.

It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.

It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.

It has also emerged that the Sussexes have changed their children's school, only days after they first started, over security concerns about the school run.

The prince previously mounted an unsuccessful legal challenge over his police security when he was visiting from the US.

But the family's return to the UK has meant a different set of circumstances for their taxpayer-funded security, and last week Ravec - which stands for the Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures - met to discuss their case.

This committee, which includes representatives of the Home Office, the police and the Royal Household, seems ready to review potential dangers.

This means a so-called Risk Management Board will consider the threats against them and the level of police protection they might need - although no final decision on the outcome has been reached.

The review will include security for their children Archie, aged seven, and Lilibet, aged five - and as first reported by HELLO! magazine, the children have switched schools from where they started earlier this month because of a security issue.

The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.

A source close to the couple said: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family.

"This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."

It is understood that Prince Harry had a review of his potential risks earlier in the summer, but before it was known that he would be returning to live in the UK.

This will be the first such security review for Meghan since she and Prince Harry ceased being working royals when they moved to the US in 2020.

Meghan posted footage on social media of the family at the weekend, showing a family outing in the countryside.

Separately on Monday, Prince Harry was told that Uganda would now take part in the Invictus Games next year.

It had appeared that Uganda was going to withdraw from the games for injured servicemen and women, in the fallout from a letter sent on behalf of King Charles emphasising that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.

The King's private secretary had spoken on the phone to Uganda's military chief, reassuring him that he approved of Uganda's participation in the games.

News.title: Farage says £72m donations are compliant 'with the law today'
News.content:
On Monday the House of Lords debated the government's Representation of the People Bill which caps the amount British people living overseas can donate to political parties at Â£100,000.

The bill also states that those who moved back to the UK would have to wait for at least a year before donating more than Â£100,000.

The legislation states that donors must have been registered as in the UK by 25 March 2026 in order to avoid the cap.

It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK.

Education Minister Georgia Gould told the BBC's Today programme the government was "really worried about the big money that is coming into politics... and sometimes money from overseas that is shaping politics rather than the ordinary voters".

She said the new rule changes had been added to the bill, following a report by former senior civil servant Sir Philip Rycroft into foreign interference in British politics, published on 25 March.

The two Â£36m donations to Reform have reignited questions about political funding.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on Radio 5 Live, Sir Philip said examining domestic donations had not been within the remit of his review but that there was a case for capping all donations, whether they came from British citizens living in the UK or overseas.

"I don't see any reason why we should have these mega sums of money coming into British politics," he said.

He added that the government's decision to retrospectively ban certain donations was "going to be controversial" but said: "If you say, you're going to change the rules to cap donations at some point in the future, then clearly the risk is that you get a lot of those donations coming through the door before you're able to do that."

Farage said the donations would allow his party to "catch up with the other big parties" and enable them to "professionalise".

He argued that trade unions gave money to Labour so that it would enact their policies and that donors gave money to the Conservative Party in order to get "knighthoods and peerages".

By contrast he said neither Harborne or Delo would get peerages or government contracts, if Reform won the next general election.

Asked if the two men had influence over Reform's policy on cryptocurrency, Farage said he had shown them his party's paper on the subject and they both "thought it made sense".

He added that the two men "will not benefit" from Reform's policies, which he said aimed to properly regulate cryptocurrency.

Farage was speaking on the same day as the Trade Unions Congress, the federation of trade unions, held its annual conference.

TUC general secretary Nowak said Reform were a "party for sale" and their donations were "a crisis for democracy".

Sharon Graham, leader of the Unite union, said the government should go further and put a cap between Â£500,000 and Â£1m on individual donations made by UK residents

Speaking on Sunday, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending. Similarly, the Green Party urged the Labour Party to "find its spine and support a tight cap".

News.title: Member of UK armed forces dies in road traffic incident in Ukraine
News.content:
A member of the UK armed forces has died in a road traffic incident in Ukraine, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) has announced.

The individual's family has been informed and has "requested a period of grace before further details are released", the MoD's statement said.

The incident on Saturday was not the result of hostile action, the BBC understands.

The British government has previously acknowledged a small number of personnel in Ukraine to support Kyiv's armed forces and provide security to diplomatic staff.

It is not known which service the individual was in or what their role was.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting shared his "deepest condolences" with their loved ones, writing on social media: "This is very sad news for the family and for those grieving with them in our armed forces."

A 28-year-old paratrooper, who died while watching the testing of a new defensive capability away from the front lines in December, was the first member of the armed forces killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.

On Sunday, a Russian drone hit and damaged a train in Yahodyn, near the Ukraine-Poland border - shortly after former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through on a different train on the same line.

The UK's national security adviser Jonathan Powell was among those on board.

No casualties were reported. Russia's defence ministry said it had struck "railway infrastructure" in western Ukraine, but Ukraine's state railway company said the drone's intended target "could have been the diplomatic train".

The UK has been one of Ukraine's closest allies during the war.

Ukraine was the location of Andy Burnham's first overseas trip as prime minister in August, where he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and promised to keep up the pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats".

Chairing his first meeting of the "coalition of the willing", set up by the UK and France under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, Burnham also agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for Scalp missiles.

News.title: Westminster's time is coming to an end, Welsh, Scottish, Northern Irish leaders say
News.content:
The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end".

The nationalist leaders from Plaid Cymru, Sinn FÃ©in and the SNP - who want their countries to leave the United Kingdom - signed an agreement on Monday which said no Westminster government had the right to "block democracy".

But while Scotland's John Swinney and Northern Ireland's Michelle O'Neill called for referendums at a joint press conference, Wales' Rhun ap Iorwerth declined to give a timetable for one in his country.

Labour and Reform accused Plaid of wanting to break up the UK.

Swinney and ap Iorwerth's governments later backed a separate agreement agreed to work together on pressing UK government on "fairness" in funding and powers.

For the first time since devolution began, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all have first ministers who want to leave the United Kingdom.

All three met on Monday as representatives of their parties. Sinn FÃ©in president Mary Lou McDonald also attended.

The memorandum of understanding said: "For people watching across these islands - for people watching around the world - there could be no clearer sign that Westminster's time is coming to an end.

"No Westminster government has the right to block democracy or undermine the principle that our people will decide their own future.

"We recognise that our parties have different constitutional positions and that each nation will determine its own future in its own way and in its own time."

News.title: Speedboat killer jailed for attack on girlfriend
News.content:
Speedboat killer Jack Shepherd has been jailed for 20 months with a further four years on extended licence for violently assaulting his girlfriend, including hitting her chest with a set of hot barbecue tongs.

The 38-year-old had pleaded guilty to two counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and damaging property at Isleworth Crown Court in July.

The attacks happened in February and June last year and sparked Shepherd's recall to prison.

He was originally jailed in 2018 for six years and six months for manslaughter over the death of 24-year-old Charlotte Brown when his speedboat crashed during a first date.

Shepherd was jailed for a further four years at Exeter Crown Court in 2019 for a drink-fuelled attack on a barman in March 2018 at a Devon hotel.

He was released on licence in January 2024, but faced recall to prison in September last year after he was accused of violence towards the woman.

According to a prosecution summary of the case, Shepherd started dating his former partner in August 2024, but towards the end of the year she accused him of being abusive and threatening.

In February 2025, he admitted pinning down the woman and "punching her several times, causing bruising to her arm and top of leg" during an argument.

In the second incident, in June 2025, Shepherd got angry with her after she said that he had burned a pizza on the barbecue, and "proceeded to hit her with the barbecue tongs on her left breast which caused a permanent scar".

News.title: No police collusion in sectarian murder but multiple RUC failings included tip-off to suspect
News.content:
An inquiry into the sectarian murder of Robert Hamill has found police officers who were in a vehicle near the attack did not condone or collude with the attackers.

However, the inquiry said there were multiple police failings in the investigation, including a tip-off to a suspect to destroy the clothing he wore that night.

The report, published on Monday, external, highlighted multiple wrongful omissions in the subsequent murder investigation including a failure to properly search the home of a key suspect.

Robert Hamill was 25 when he died after he was beaten by loyalists in Portadown, County Armagh, in 1997.

The inquiry concluded in 2009 and its report was completed in 2011 but the findings could not be published until three prosecutions in connection with the case concluded.

The inquiry concluded: "We find that Robert Hamill had been assaulted before the Land Rover officers got out of their vehicle.

"However, they were not aware of the assault and after they had got out of their vehicle, they attempted to restore order.

"They did not in any way condone or collude with attackers."

Although the inquiry found that the four officers in the police Land Rover could not have prevented the murder, the police investigation was flawed â both at the scene and in the days that followed.

"The inquiry found that serving RUC [Royal Ulster Constabulary] officers were guilty of wrongful omissions and that those omissions arose both at the scene and during the initial investigation," it said.

The inquiry concluded that some of the mistakes in the investigation were negligent, while others were deliberate.

The 290-page report followed an inquiry which cost approximately Â£33m.

The actions of the officers in the Land Rover have been the subject of many claims and counter-claims in the past three decades.

Given how close they were to the scene, questions have been asked about why they did not intervene sooner.

The inquiry found that they were "distracted talking to two members of the public".

On whether they could have done more, the three-person inquiry panel did not have a unanimous view.

Two members concluded that the officers in the police vehicle were not guilty "of any wrongful act or omission in relation to the death of Robert Hamill".

However, on this issue the chairperson Sir Edwin Jowitt "expressed a dissenting view".

News.title: British Crown symbol was branded on enslaved Africans, research finds
News.content:
Enslaved African people were branded with an identifying mark that included an emblem of the British Crown, according to new research by a project documenting British involvement in the slave trade.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the Register of British Slave Traders research, described the imprinting as a "dramatic and harrowing" symbol of the monarchy's relationship to slavery.

The register, external lists 13,000 individuals and hundreds of institutions known to have invested in Britain's role in slavery between 1563 and 1807, when the trade was abolished across the British Empire.

Researchers say it is the most comprehensive examination of a national community of slave traders ever undertaken.

Dr Nicholas Radburn, historian at Lancaster University and co-investigator in the project, told the BBC he first found the identifying mark - which is an image of the Crown, with the South Sea Company logo below it - while looking through the company's archives at the British Library in 2022.

Founded in 1711, the South Sea Company was set up as a public and private British company and trafficked thousands of enslaved Africans.

Radburn said it was "remarkable" to find records of the branding "buried in a very nondescript sounding volume: 'The Register of Instruments'".

In 2024, he found letters that helped piece the story together. They were from the company's director to their "factors" (slave traders) in the Spanish Americas, Radburn explained.

"The letters were full of very detailed instructions on how to conduct the slave trade," he recalled.

One letter from February 1714 was "exceptional because it laid bare so clearly the ways in which the London-based directors were personally involved in the violence that was committed against the enslaved in the Americas".

The directors sent irons made in England for slave traders to use to mark enslaved African people on their left shoulder with the emblem.

The purpose, the letter outlined, was to distinguish the company's slaves from others.

In an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Pettigrew - from King's College London - said there were all sorts of connections between the monarchy and slavery, not just this "brutal imprint".

"If you think about the history of the monarchy when it was at its absolute lowest ebb, when King Charles I was executed, members of the royal family relaunched the monarchy, its finances and its reputation, by investing in the transatlantic slave trade," he said.

He said it was important to draw a distinction between the monarchy as an institution, and the individuals who led it.

"The institution is the same as it was hundreds of years ago.

"So when we talk about the role of the slave trade in rehabilitating the monarchy or improving its position, we're talking about an institution that is still very much a part of British life today.

"In a court of law, the monarchy is the same institution today as it was in the 17th Century."

In a statement, Buckingham Palace said King Charles "has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today".

The King is "grateful to all those undertaking academic work in this area and thus contributing to the debate about how such issues might best be addressed".

News.title: Police officer who put suspect in headlock and punched him 9 times faces misconduct hearing
News.content:
A police officer who punched a suspect nine times in the head used unreasonable force on multiple occasions, a police misconduct hearing has been told.

PC Richard Williams faces eight allegations relating to the arrest of Steven Clark, including using a headlock or "choker", unreasonable use of incapacitant spray, and throwing or dropping Clark into the back of a police van.

A misconduct hearing at North Wales Police headquarters in Colwyn Bay heard Williams denies wrongdoing.

He was cleared of assault and intentional strangulation following a seven-day trial in Caernarfon, Gwynedd, in 2025.

In May 2023, police were called to Porthmadog in Gwynedd, following a report of a domestic argument.

A woman told officers, Clark, then 34, was "off his head on wacky backy" and possibly other drugs.

The misconduct hearing was played several clips of police body-worn camera footage, as well as mobile phone video recorded by onlookers.

When police tried to arrest Clark, the misconduct hearing was told things "take a turn", and the suspect ended up on the ground.

It is alleged Williams used handcuffs to "cause pain to Clark's wrist", who "winced and reacted".

News.title: This is what women in sport look like - female athletes hit back
News.content:
Female athletes have spoken out against a controversial sports gambling advert starring actress Sydney Sweeney.

The advert has gone viral online and features American Sweeney naked but covering parts of her body with various pieces of sporting equipment.

It has sparked a strong reaction, with many female athletes criticising its sexualisation of women in sport, and how they are being defined by their appearance rather than their achievements as sportswomen.

Amy Hunt, who became a four-time European champion earlier this summer, referenced the advert after she ran a season's best 22.10 seconds to finish fourth in the 200m final at the Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Sunday.

"Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," Hunt said in her post-race interview with BBC Sport.

Referring to Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's winning time of 21.47 seconds, the fourth fastest ever over the distance, she added: "21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening."

American actress Sweeney, 29, starred in the television series Euphoria and her films include Anyone But You and The Housemaid.

The backlash has included many other athletes from a range of sports posting videos of themselves competing or training, and describing the frustrations and struggles they have faced throughout their careers.

The trend was started by American gymnast Gracie Kramer, who posted a montage of herself training with the caption, "I don't know what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what women in sport look like."

Kramer told BBC World Service's Newshour show she "did not expect" the reaction to her post and "just wanted to uplift women and remind them that you may see these types of ads but remember that this is not the only thing that matters".

She said it was "so cool" to see "all the incredible athletes hopping on this trend, uplifting themselves, uplifting each other", adding she was used to getting "very demeaning and objectifying" messages from men because of competing in a leotard as a gymnast.

Kramer added: "Unfortunately being objectified pretty much my entire career, it made me feel strong enough to post about this and to stand up for the women that don't want to be objectified and don't want to be looped into this unfortunate narrative that's been pushed for a long time."

High-profile figures including presenter Jeremy Clarkson and former prime minister Lord Cameron have earned praise for "shining a light" on prostate cancer, helping to persuade more men to evaluate their health risk.

Their openness sparked a "Clarkson-Cameron effect", prompting a sharp rise in individuals accessing Prostate Cancer UK’s 30-second online risk checker following the disclosures.

According to the charity, numerous men have reached out after being moved to check their own status by these public personal accounts.

This surge in checks has, in certain instances, resulted in a timely diagnosis that "saved their life".

Speaking about sharing his experience on an episode of Clarkson’s Farm, Clarkson remarked that doing so was "worthwhile" provided his story "gets even one bloke to stop ignoring the issue and do something about it".

Former prime minister David Cameron, who revealed in 2025 he had prostate cancer ( PA )

Now in remission, the 66-year-old disclosed during the latest series that he had been diagnosed with an "aggressive" form of the condition.

Meanwhile, Lord Cameron said that he “wholeheartedly supports all efforts to raise awareness” of the disease.

New figures from Prostate Cancer UK show that nearly 50,880 men completed its online risk checker in the week after Clarkson revealed his diagnosis, up from 8,425 men the previous week.

Clarkson said: “I feel incredibly lucky that my cancer was caught early.

“It’s why I’m still here today, feeling fine and looking forward to seeing my grandchildren grow up.

“I’ve always said that if my story gets even one bloke to stop ignoring the issue and do something about it, then it’s been worthwhile.

“To hear that actually tens of thousands of men have already taken the risk checker is something to be hugely proud of.

“But there’s still plenty more to do. So, I’ll keep saying it: if you’re a man, check your risk. It only takes a couple of minutes and it could save your life.”

Meanwhile, 22,562 men took the risk checker the day after Lord Cameron’s announcement, up from 2,175 the previous Monday.

Lord Cameron said: “Prostate cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer for men in the UK, so it is vital that men are aware of their own risk profile.

“This is particularly important as, regrettably, we do not yet have a proper, national, targeted screening programme that involves all those at higher risk.

“As such, I wholeheartedly support all efforts to raise awareness. Prostate Cancer UK’s risk checker is a quick and simple online tool that I encourage all men to use.

“Catching cancers early is the best possible way to boost the chances of successful treatment like I received, so being aware of your risk to the disease is essential.”

The charity also highlighted how 280,000 men checked their risk in the two months after Sir Chris Hoy’s diagnosis.

Prostate Cancer UK said that since its online risk checker was launched in 2020 it can been completed by more than five million men.

Amy Rylance, director of health services, equity and improvement at Prostate Cancer UK, said: “Prostate cancer is the most common cancer in the UK, but too many men are still being diagnosed by chance and, sadly, often too late for a cure.

“Our risk checker helps men navigate this complex disease, empowering men with a clear way to understand their risk and their choices.

“We hear from so many men who say a celebrity diagnosis, like Jeremy Clarkson or Lord Cameron’s, inspired them to check their risk and in some cases saved their life.

“We’re extremely grateful to everyone who has publicly shared their experiences of prostate cancer, shining a light onto this disease that is much easier to treat when found earlier, and kickstarting many lifesaving conversations.

“We know men need a safe and effective screening programme. Prostate Cancer UK’s Transform trial will get us the evidence we need to make this a reality and give every man the chance for an early diagnosis.

“Until then, public figures telling their stories and inspiring men to check their risk are playing an important role in helping men and loved ones across the country, and we thank them for their vital work.”

Eye scans could assist in identifying a widespread heart condition that heightens stroke risks years before diagnosis, a study has found.

Researchers said the technique provides a non-invasive method to alert patients to atrial fibrillation (AF) prior to it "causes real harm".

Scientists analysed records from over 90,000 individuals and discovered that those affected possessed distinct biological markers in their retina, the light-sensitive tissue layer in the eye that detects light and converts it into signals for the brain.

Around 1.5 million people in the UK are estimated to have AF, which brings about an irregular heartbeat, though hundreds of thousands more may be living undiagnosed.

AF sometimes presents without symptoms and is intermittent, meaning it can be missed during diagnostic heart checks known as electrocardiograms (ECGs).

open image in gallery Moorfields Eye Hospital of John Brewer (right) with Josef Huemer, consultant ophthalmologist at Moorfields Eye Hospital. Mr Brewer discovered he had AF during cataract surgery at the hospital ( PA )

Although the condition is not directly life-threatening, it can produce blood clots that lead to strokes.

Researchers at Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and UCL Institute of Ophthalmology looked at data from 50,651 taking part in the AlzEye study and 39,013 people from the UK Biobank.

In total, some 6,261 patients already had AF.

The analysis found that these people tended to have thinner retinal layers.

Patients who did not have AF at the time their eye scans were taken but went on to develop the condition also had thinner retinal layers four years prior to attending hospital on average.

Moorfields patient John Brewer, from Croydon, discovered he had AF while having surgery to remove cataracts earlier this year.

When the team noticed his heartbeat was unsteady he was given an ECG and medicine to allow the operation to continue, and a cardiologist later confirmed the diagnosis.

Mr Brewer said: “It would have been so much easier if my AF had been detected earlier through a routine retinal scan at one of my regular appointments, rather than on the operating table, which was a very distressing experience for my wife and I.”

Experts suggest that while eye scans would not replace ECGs to diagnose AF, they could be a “complementary tool”.

Siegfried Wagner, of UCL, said: “This large-scale analysis shows that retinal imaging can pick up on structural changes within the eye that are clearly linked to AF.

“For patients, the value of this kind of eye imaging is that it is easy to access, quick and doesn’t involve any invasive procedures.

“Although not intended to replace ECG-based diagnosis, retinal imaging could act as a complementary tool, catching those most at risk of AF before it causes real harm.”

Lead author Josef Huemer, consultant ophthalmologist at Moorfields Eye Hospital, said: “If confirmed in further research, our findings raise the possibility that routine eye examinations could, in future, help identify people who would benefit from closer cardiac assessment, potentially enabling earlier treatment with therapies known to reduce the risk of stroke.”

The findings have been published in the journal Plos Digital Health.

Pubs and retail outlets will be permitted to accept digital ID as valid proof of age when purchasing alcohol under new laws.

The policy provides a modern alternative to carrying physical identity documents, enabling customers to use their mobile phones to verify their age in pubs, live concerts and festivals.

Taking effect on Tuesday, these statutory updates to the licensing act apply across commercial businesses in England and Wales.

However, officials anticipate that widespread adoption of the technology will take some time.

The digital proof will be delivered via third-party software such as Yoti, a service already deployed in specific contexts, such as verifying young filmgoers buying age-restricted cinema tickets.

Ministers intend to broaden digital age verification past retail alcohol purchases, targeting sales of tobacco products and vaping devices as the next immediate priority.

The move follows Prime Minister Andy Burnham cancelling a broader national digital ID project originally formulated during the tenure of his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.

open image in gallery A bark worker pours a pint of Guinness at the bar in pub ( AFP/Getty )

Digital Government Minister Stephanie Peacock said: “From pubs and restaurants to music venues and festivals, licensed businesses carry out millions of age checks every year.

“It will remain an individual or business’ choice whether to use or adopt it, and physical ID will remain a valid way for customers to prove their age.

“This groundbreaking change in the law will mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information such as your name or address just to prove your age – allowing everyone to feel safer on a night out.”

Those buying alcohol will need to go through an authentication process to prove it is their ID each time they use it – for example by scanning their face or entering a code on the app.

This will then generate a token, such as a QR code, that remains valid for a window of around 30 seconds to guard against someone falsely using another person’s ID.

In some cases the user might enter a pin to verify themselves, with a photo then sent to a terminal that the bartender or person behind a till could use to compare to the person in front of them.

Several third-party apps are expected to be available.

open image in gallery Digital Government Minister Stephanie Peacock ( Chris McAndrew/PA )

The Government has asked developers to make their systems interoperable so customers can have one ID app on their phone rather than being forced to download multiple apps to use at different retailers.

It is expected to be available to use offline in the same way contactless payments can be.

It is not yet clear what the cost to businesses will be, but it is thought that it will be possible to integrate the technology into tablets they already own.

Businesses are not legally required to keep accepting physical ID for alcohol purchases as the licensing changes give equivalence to digital and physical forms.

But the Government does not expect them to stop taking physical IDs as doing so would exclude some customers and there is no cost to continuing to accept them.

Allen Simpson, chief executive of industry group UKHospitality, said:

“Introducing digital proof of age is a positive step for hospitality, providing greater flexibility and convenience for customers and businesses.

“The roll-out of the voluntary digital proof of age will provide an easier experience for customers, allowing them to verify their age securely from their phones.

“We look forward to working with the Government to ensure the roll-out of the scheme, with multiple supplier options available, is cost-efficient and not burdensome for the hospitality sector.”

Nearly two in five small British businesses were hit by a cyber attack in the past year at a cost of nearly £27,000 each, according to new research.

The latest annual Hiscox Cyber Readiness Report shows 38% of small firms in the UK say they suffered a successful hack within the last 12 months.

The report – based on results of a global survey of nearly 7,000 cybersecurity decision-makers in smaller firms, including 1,000 in the UK – found British firms were the most vulnerable among their global counterparts, with 29% worldwide saying they were hit by a successful cyber attack.

Those affected globally reported an average of four cyber attack incidents over the same period.

In the UK, the cost of each cyber attack was 35,908 US dollars on average (£26,650), according to the study.

Cyber incidents now cost firms worldwide around 52,000 US dollars a year on average (£38,604) and cause around 32 hours of operational disruption, it found.

But the survey shows the impacts can be far-reaching, with almost one in three (32%) of companies worldwide saying it delayed growth and expansion plans, and similar results for those saying it increased staffing costs (31%), caused financial damage (30%) and saw business opportunities lost (29%).

And more than a quarter of those impacted by a hack also faced financial penalties (28%), or bad publicity (26%).

Firms are spending significant sums to ward off the threat of hacks, with the study revealing the average UK small firm spend on resilience measures is now 59,700 dollars (£44,294) – the third highest worldwide and above the 51,000 US dollar (£38,000) global average.

There is also an increasing trend to link pay for top bosses to cybersecurity, with 25% of small UK firms now doing so, and 32% worldwide.

Eddie Lamb, global head of cyber at Hiscox, said: “During our 20-plus years of insuring cyber risks and our decade of cyber readiness research, we’ve seen a clear shift in the cyber threat and how businesses respond to it.

“Cyber risk has become a recurring cost, not an exceptional event, so the investment we’re seeing in cyber resilience is good news as businesses start to take back control.”

Reading for pleasure offers significant health benefits no matter the material chosen, according to scientists from the University of Cambridge.

In a newly published review, researchers outline how reading enhances mental wellbeing, improves educational outcomes, fosters empathy and reduces the likelihood of developing dementia.

The findings, authored by Professor Barbara Sahakian and Dr Christelle Langley from Cambridge’s department of psychiatry, were featured in the journal Psychological Medicine.

Their work aligns with the National Year of Reading, with the academics partnering with The Queen’s Reading Room, a charity established by the Queen to promote the advantages of literature.

Highlighted in the review is a study involving over 10,000 young people, which found that children taking up recreational reading early display enhanced memory, concentration, and executive functioning such as problem solving.

Furthermore, these young readers achieve higher marks, suffer from fewer mental health difficulties, and maintain healthier habits, enjoying increased sleep and reduced screen time.

Dr Langley said: “Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading.

“The important thing is to find something they’d really enjoy reading about – it might be a TV programme or a game – and use this as a way in.

“Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels.”

Overall, the study found that reading at any age improves brain and mental health, leads to better cognitive performance and reduces the risk of mental decline.

One study found that children who begin reading for pleasure early in life have a better attention span, memory, and executive functioning ( Getty Images )

“Survey data in adults suggested that reading was associated with reduced stress, greater empathy, enhanced wellbeing, and decreased loneliness,” the study said.

“Studies further indicate that cognitively stimulating activities, particularly reading, are associated with a lower risk of dementia and slower cognitive decline, even among individuals with lower educational attainment….

“Neuroimaging findings suggest that reading is associated with structural and functional differences in brain regions supporting executive control, emotional regulation, and social cognition. Importantly, these benefits appear independent of socioeconomic background.”

Book clubs also promote social connection, it said.

Prof Sahakian said: “Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction.

“They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia.

“While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they’re perfect for older people who may be not so mobile – they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy.”

Prof Sahakian added that “it’s never too late to start” reading, and “it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age”.

Data suggests that reading among children and teenagers is at its lowest levels since records began, particularly among those from disadvantaged backgrounds.

A recent study from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development on 760,000 students in 91 countries found 15-year-olds have worse reading skills than at any point this century, and maths and science is being pulled down with it.

It found the average student is reading at a level once expected of someone a year younger.

In the new review, one study of almost 5,500 adults aged 55 and older found those engaged in things like reading were significantly less likely to develop cognitive impairment over a five-year follow-up.

Another study found that reading newspapers, magazines and books was linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease.

Previous research from the Queen’s Reading Room also found that five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20% as well as boosting concentration and problem-solving skills, and helping readers feel less lonely.

Vicki Perrin, chief executive of the Queen’s Reading Room, said: “Books truly do make life better and we’re excited to do our bit to help everyone, everywhere, make more room for reading.”

News.title: Newcastle rocked and Elland Road rocking after Leeds complete demolition job
News.content:
The foundations are being put in around the stadium for a cavernous new West Stand, and Farke’s remit is to ensure that Leeds will be firmly established in the Premier League by the time it is completed in the summer of 2028.

To be fair to Farke, he has laid a sturdy base for this team to thrive and it felt before kick-off that this was going to be a big evening for Leeds, who had made a quietly encouraging start to the campaign and had negotiated three challenging away trips without defeat.

Big? It turned out to be spectacular. The first half was so one-sided that a boxing referee would not have allowed Newcastle to come out for the second, such was the pummelling they received; wave after wave of white-shirted raids left the visitors black and blue.

Aside from one little rick inside the opening 10 minutes, when James Trafford dithered and presented Yoane Wissa with a chance to mug him, Leeds were every bit as sensational as Newcastle were shocking, seizing on the opportunity to go on a rampage.

Leeds would have been in front after 11 minutes but Ethan Ampadu’s fierce drive battered into Calvert-Lewin’s legs and bounced away. Normally in such circumstances, players will wave an arm to berate their bad luck, but Ampadu, celebrating his 26th birthday, smiled: he, like everyone else, sensed what was coming.

Jayden Bogle, Justin and Nico Elvedi all had opportunities to open the scoring earlier, but eventually, they found the weak spot. Newcastle, who had lost the influential Nico González to a potential concussion, had replaced him with Sean Steur and what an influence he would have on matters.

On the half hour, Steur was a fraction too late getting out to close down Tanaka, whose shot ricocheted off him and to Lewis Miley, before looping away from Lukas Hornicek and dropping into the corner of the net in dam-busting fashion.

News.title: Wall Street hit by tech sell-off after AI bosses push for slowdown
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Tech stocks have fallen sharply after Elon Musk and the boss of OpenAI joined calls for the slowdown of AI development. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Hundreds of hotels, pubs and restaurants urge Burnham to slash VAT | Prime Minister challenged to honour pledge to cut levy to 10pc and save thousands of jobs

2) Trump rejects Silicon Valley’s calls for AI slowdown | US president says ‘very negative forces’ are overstating the risks

3) Labour’s wealth raid ‘kills off ultra-luxury homes in London’ | A 120-home project in St John’s Wood is likely to be the last residence of its kind

4) Factories slash hiring ahead of Budget | Manufacturing vacancies fall by 6.2pc, despite rising business confidence

5) David Lloyd waters down net zero targets | Gym chain has spent millions on solar panels and heat pumps in effort to cut emissions

What happened overnight

Asian stocks fell as traders assessed fresh safety concerns over the pace of AI development.

South Korea’s Kospi lost 3.3pc to 6,679.23 and Japan’s Nikkei 225 index slid 0.6pc to 63,633.57. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.3pc to 24,886.81.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq index dropped 1.2pc in Asian trading hours, while S&P 500 futures shed 0.5pc. Those linked to The Dow Jones Industrial Average were down 0.1pc.

It came despite efforts from Donald Trump to downplay concerns about AI technology, saying on Sunday that “very negative forces” were overstating the risks.

On Saturday, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for tech companies to slow down their advancement and for more work to be done on AI safety. His comments were backed by Sam Altman, the OpenAI boss, Sir Demis Hassabis, the chairman of Google DeepMind, and Elon Musk.

Oil rose after Saudi Arabia was forced to close a crucial oil pipeline after drone attacks from Iraq on Friday. Brent crude was up 2.8pc to $107.5 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate rose 2.22pc to $102.3 a barrel.

The US’s 10-year Treasury yields edged closer to the crucial 5pc level on Friday amid the prolonged bond sell-off, while two-year yields climbed to 4.66pc.

News.title: The best pubs with rooms in Kent
News.content:
All our reviewers are either resident destination experts or travel writers that specialise in hotels. Often they will have stayed at a hotel many times and so can see how it has changed for better or worse over the years. They know what makes a great hotel in that particular destination and will compare it contextually against local competition. When our reviewers first visit a hotel, they stay for at least one night, eat one meal in addition to breakfast and will experience all of the facilities on offer. Whichever category of room they stay in, they will see the entry-level rooms in order to assess them.



After their stay, our reviewers then give the hotel six scores out of 10, rating its location, style and character, service and facilities, rooms, food and drink, and value for money. The average of these scores then determines the overall score. Our experts then select reviews for curated lists like this – the best hotels in a particular destination for families, for instance – together with the Telegraph Hotels team.

News.title: Asia on high alert as El Niño threatens new Dengue epidemic
News.content:
Countries from Brazil to Taiwan are bracing for a surge in dengue driven by the “supersized” El Niño, as the UN warns this year’s weather phenomenon could be the strongest on record.

Both the virus and the Aedes mosquitoes that transmit it are especially sensitive to heat – and the El Niño is expected to push global temperatures to new highs.

“El Niño is being supersized before our eyes,” Antonio Guterres, the UN Secretary General, said last week. “The ​science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.”

The weather phenomenon – a periodic warming of sea surface temperature in the eastern Pacific, caused by weakening trade winds – alters rainfall and temperature patterns across the globe. That, in turn, causes extreme weather like droughts, heatwaves, floods and typhoons – which then trigger events including wildfires, crop failures and a collapse in affected fisheries.

But it can also have a major impact on the transmission of disease, including dengue – and countries across the world, especially in Asia and Latin America, are bracing for outbreaks.

In July, Brazil’s Ministry of Health sent an alert warning states that arboviruses like dengue, chikungunya and Zika could surge later this year, and urged officials to ramp up disease surveillance and mosquito control programmes.

The increase will likely peak in 2027: the biomedical research institute Fiocruz has estimated that Brazil will see 1.7 million dengue cases next year, driven by El Niño.

News.title: ‘Your home is your palace’: Queen Elizabeth II’s housekeeper answers reader questions
News.content:
Was there one surprisingly simple trick used in the palace that made things feel instantly more polished?

Jay, West Midlands

Making sure you have a routine is the best way for everything to feel polished. At the palace, the team is trained, and everyone has the right tools and time to do their job... They learned how to lift things safely and how to be confident when they were around the Royal Collection. When you’re cleaning historic areas such as palaces and castles, you have to make sure you don’t overdo it. We had a daily routine that ensured we didn’t over-clean everything.

What is the royal protocol for dealing with ironing and maintaining perfectly crisp sheets without using harsh, eco-unfriendly chemicals?

Saleem, London

Much of what would be classed as royal protocol are things we would do in our own homes. For linen, you need to treat it well and look after it by not washing it at too high a temperature or using too much detergent. Make sure the products you’re using are eco-friendly, not only for the environment, but also to care for the linen. For historic linen, it needs to be handled very gently, as it can tear quite easily.

Did the Queen get involved in any of the details of housekeeping?

Peter, East of England

I was very blessed. The Queen did leave it up to me to make those decisions because she trusted me to keep her home and the other royal residences clean and up to a great standard. I kept in touch with her, making sure the team was involved. We would have regular update meetings to ensure everyone knew what was happening and when. There was planned cleaning throughout the year depending on what was occurring, making sure certain areas were protected or closed off, for example.

I would feel very stressed cleaning around objects of great value, history and sentiment. How do you avoid disasters?

Catherine, North West

It’s important the team feels confident when cleaning those areas. We achieve that through training and building their confidence.

In the castle, we introduced a cleaning schedule that covered different areas within the state apartments – and it meant that we didn’t over-clean. The structure of this schedule was important. Every day, we would ensure we vacuumed and damp-dusted; there were no actual chemicals or any what I call “wet chemicals”. On a Monday, for instance, we would clean vases. On a Tuesday, we would do the fireplaces. On a Wednesday, it would be light fittings.

It’s crucial the team is given the right amount of time to clean, so that they don’t feel rushed or stressed. But we also have to remember that accidents happen. And if an accident happens and it was just an accident, then what can you do? It’s just one of those things.

Ultimately, making sure people are trained and confident is the key.

With limited time, what are the housekeeping priorities?

David, South West

My housekeeping priorities when at home are to make things look really tidy quickly. Putting your newspapers away, fluffing the cushions up, tidying the curtains, making sure your washing is cleared and the dishwasher is on – these are all things that will make a big difference, even if you haven’t had time to get your mop or vacuum out.

When are you satisfied a room is clean?

D, North West

I am quite a hard taskmaster and I do like perfection, but equally, that comes with making sure people understand the guidelines and what’s expected of them, after being trained properly.

I like to be visible and around the team, showing them what I’m looking at. I would get them to sit on a toilet and then shut the door, so they could see what’s behind the door – or sit in the bath, because that way you can see what other people are seeing when they’re using it. If you’re cleaning and rushing around, you don’t always see those little details.

News.title: Woeful Man Utd have no excuses, Carrick is under big pressure
News.content:
Afterwards Haaland talked about City’s “personality, character” and that was exactly what United lacked. They did not adapt a tactical plan to combat 10-man City’s desire to keep their wingers high and wide, and break with intent and still try and attack.

It was telling that so little did City’s new head coach Enzo Maresca worry about United that he did not add a defensive player, and when he took off Rayan Cherki at half-time, he replaced him with the equally creative Iliman Ndiaye who impressed. Maresca knew United needed space to run in behind and denied them that. It was that simple.

City also struck the post with United goalkeeper Senne Lammens tipping an Enzo Fernández shot against the frame of the goal, and the visitors were worthy winners as they preserved their perfect start to the season to draw level on points with leaders, Arsenal.

City handled the occasion and the – admittedly toothless – opposition superbly under their new head coach and will clearly be Arsenal’s closest challengers this season.

Maresca delivered a masterclass. For Carrick? This was a disasterclass. An object lesson in how not to use a man-advantage. And now United will have to endure even more City songs after being outplayed at home like this.

Was it complacency? Was it inability? Was it a damning lack of courage, confidence, belief even? On the pitch and in the dugout United were far too passive. This was not how a big team plays and Carrick needs to wake up.

The former midfielder did so well last season to guide United into Champions League qualification but so far this campaign he has given the impression that his job is done. Rather than that the real work starts now.

News.title: Redemption Sunday for Hull and Woad as Europe reclaim Solheim Cup
News.content:
The quiet but steely 22-year-old, who everyone seemed to have forgotten was a rookie, punched her fist when she held the decisive two-footer, before the customary hug with opponent Auston Kim and then being mobbed by her team.

“This was really important,” Woad said. “I mean, I was pretty disappointed and felt like I was kind of letting everyone down. Then the captain kind of spoke to me and said that I was third on [the most] birdies [made]. So I just had to trust that and that’s golf sometimes. And it ended up I got the winning putt.”

Some will claim that Woad was only the match-winner on a technicality. Carlota Ciganda in the penultimate game had not finished off her win against Jennifer Kupcho, but when Woad tapped in, the Spaniard was three up with three to go and was guaranteed a half. So the acclaim Woad received was granted. Not that anyone in the Europe camp cared.

The previous evening they had returned to their team room feeling slightly down that they did not hold the advantage, Kupcho holing a 91-footer on the 17th and a 30-footer on the 18th to deny Ciganda and Céline Boutier. And their mood was not helped when videos appeared on social media of the Americans taking crates of beer on to the bus back to their hotel. Yet that foolish scenario only offered extra incentive. “At least we’ll be the ones taking crates of beer on to our bus this evening,” Mel Reid, the assistant captain, said quite pointedly.

News.title: Lando Norris fumes at virtual safety car rules for costing him Spanish GP win
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the 2026 Spanish Grand Prix, the first time the race has been held at the all-new, purpose-built street circuit, the Madring. The track has developed a reputation in its short life for being a bit of a tricky one. Some have gone so far as to call it a “car killer”? Is it living up to that reputation? Probably, especially if you look at some of the lower formulae that have run on it.

It has also increasingly become the case for the Formula One cars, too. The first couple of practice sessions on Friday revealed little to worry about. As the drivers began to push, though, from final practice and qualifying, the mistakes and crashes happened. The biggest so far was Oliver Bearman but also a smaller one for Lewis Hamilton.

There will almost certainly be some kind of incident in the race, but whether we see red flags, safety cars and so on remains to be seen. A bigger and perhaps more significant question will be how much overtaking will take place on this track. The drivers are not optimistic. The theory goes that if tyre degradation is high then there will be, because you will have significant pace offsets between worn and fresh tyres. The problem is that the leaders tend not to differ to greatly from one another on strategy these days...

Perhaps George Russell, who qualified down in sixth and has little to lose, will be brave and put on a set of hard tyres to start with. Russell has work to do yet again. He was not miles off Antonelli in qualifying when it came to pace, but given how close it was in the top six, finds four cars between himself and the championship leader, who just missed out on pole to McLaren’s Lando Norris.

Norris said it was the best lap of his life and seemed to come from nowhere. He improved more than a second from Q2 to Q3 and continues his fine form in 2026. He will start alongside Antonelli with Max Verstappen in third, Lewis Hamilton in fourth and Charles Leclerc in fifth, before Russell.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta sends warning to Max Dowman, 16, after wonderkid was left out of Arsenal squad and dropped down to U21s
Sports.content:
MIKEL ARTETA has warned Max Dowman he must “earn” his minutes like “anybody else” after leaving the wonderkid out of his matchday squad.

Dowman, 16, was left out of Arteta’s squad to face Sunderland at the weekend and instead played the full 90 minutes for the Gunners’ Under-21s against Chelsea.



It was the second time that Dowman has been part of the U21 side this season, despite a breakout campaign last term.

The teenager is yet to get any senior minutes this season and although Arteta has promised those chances will come, he reiterated that Dowman must work hard to earn them.



The Arsenal boss said: “I wish we could have him [against Sunderland], but we have the limitation with the numbers that we can have.

Dowman became the Premier League’s youngest ever player and youngest ever goalscorer last season as he burst onto the scene in North London.

And the record-breaker could be given the nod for the first time this term when Arsenal take on Ipswich Town in the League Cup third round on Tuesday.

Arteta knows that he has to rotate his squad this season if he wants to go deep in all competitions, having suffered defeat to Manchester City in last season’s League Cup final.

Sports.title: Leeds 4 Newcastle 1: Calvert-Lewin stakes England claim as Daniel Farke’s men run riot to hammer Toon
Sports.content:
RED-HOT Leeds smashed Matthias Jaissle’s unbeaten Newcastle record to pieces with an electrifying first-half display.

The Mags were waving the white flag by the break after Lewis Miley’s own-goal before Jayden Bogle and Dominic Calvert-Lewin blew them away.



And Jaissle’s former Red Bull Salzburg star Noah Okafor rubbed more salt in the wounds in the second half to round-off the 4-1 thumping.

German Jaissle’s honeymoon is well and truly over, but compatriot Daniel Farke has Whites fans dreaming of Europe as they climbed into third.



Four matches undefeated. A captain in Ethan Ampadu who continues to grow into a midfield monster. And, most importantly, an England striker in Calvert-Lewin who cannot stop scoring.

Despite the huge summer of change at Newcastle, some things remain the same. And Jaissle will be just as sick of the sight of him as the Toon Army.

This was Calvert-Lewin’s eighth career goal against the Magpies – his most against any opponent.

He and Leeds were just too hot to handle for the shellshocked Toon, who appeared to be flying under the new man. But the numbers have told a different story.



His side have been playing with fire all this season and they finally got burned in West Yorkshire.

Newcastle had conceded a worrying 61 shots in their opening three Prem games. Fortunately, £25.7million summer signing Lukas Hornicek got to work fast, making 13 saves across those matches.

SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

But despite several more spectacular ones here, the Czech keeper was powerless to stop the Leeds storm.

The bright lights of Elland Road were always going to be Jaissle’s toughest test yet. Leeds have been formidable here since Farke’s arrival in 2023, suffering just one defeat now in 26 evening league kick offs.

That has earned the nickname “Farke After Dark” amongst Leeds supporters. And on this form, it could be European nights soon.



Jaissle, who confirmed in-form winger Anthony Elanga could be out long-term before kick-off with an unspecified injury, also lost £48m midfielder Nico Gonzalez to a head injury midway through the half.

But their downfall had already begun. Their £51m forward Matias Fernandez-Pardo was lucky to avoid a nightmare debut when he went unpunished for palming the ball away in his own box with less than a minute on the clock.

Hornicek saved his side with a brilliant scoop away from Jayden Bogle’s close-range spin and turn before tipping over the wing-back’s volley.



But Ao Tanaka’s strike first hit Sean Steur – on for Gonzalez – and then Lewis Miley, wrong-footing Hornicek as he stood powerless and watched the ball hit the net.

Moments later it was two and another nightmare for Steur. His underhit pass was pounced on by Bogle.

Within a flash it was worked wide and Calvert-Lewin and Bogle both rose about Sven Botman, the former’s header hitting the latter and going in.

The floodgates were open and Leeds smelt blood. Hornicek’s double save prevented Ampadu and DCL but there was no stopping the hotshot on the stroke of half time.

He sent Botman to the papershop when dragging it back on his right foot before pulling the trigger, the shot taking a slight knick off Malick Thiaw on its way in.



This was the first time Leeds had scored three in the first half of a Premier League game at home since May 2001.



That day they got five against Bradford and they quickly set about adding to their tally following the restart.

It was four with half an hour to go when Newcastle failed to clear a long throw. It dropped for Okafor, and he lashed home a half-volley past the diving Hornicek.

That was the icing on the cake for the Whites and Farke.
