World.title: Iran envoy: Georgia not the only destination for Iranians
World.content:
Iranian envoy to Georgia makes pointed remarks

Iranian Ambassador to Georgia Seyed Ali Moujani has responded to a statement by Georgia’s Civil Aviation Agency saying the country would fully comply with sanctions against Iranian airlines imposed by the United States. The ambassador said Georgia had been one possible destination for Iranians, but was not the only one.

On 8 September, the United States imposed sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines. Six of them — Sepehran Airlines, Varesh Airlines, Qeshm Air, Fly Kish Airlines, Taban Airlines and AVA Airlines — also operate flights between Georgia and Iran. “As the expanded sanctions list announced by the US State Department includes airlines that currently operate flights between Georgia and Iran, the Georgian side, as in other cases, will act in full compliance with the international sanctions regime,” the Civil Aviation Agency said.

In turn, the Iranian embassy published a map of the Black Sea region showing only half of Georgia. When the Georgian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty asked the Iranian ambassador whether the map was intended to convey a political message, he replied:

“Sometimes a diplomat can say nothing, write nothing and simply share a picture… Water knows no borders; the Caucasus and Iran need a common, interconnected future.”

Map published by Iranian ambassador to Georgia

What Iran’s ambassador said

Seyed Ali Moujani said Iranian tour operators had contacted the embassy’s consular section in recent days with questions about whether tourist trips to Georgia would continue.

“Georgia has undoubtedly been one of the important Black Sea tourist destinations for Iranians,” Moujani wrote, noting that the country had attracted many Iranian tourists in recent years.

He also said Iran respected Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s independent decisions.

“Georgia’s recent decision to introduce certain restrictions in connection with Western sanctions is one that we must respect as the country’s choice. However, respecting the choices of others does not mean disregarding our own right to choose,” the Iranian ambassador wrote.

Moujani said Iranian tourists, like citizens of other countries, considered a range of factors when choosing a holiday destination, including safety, convenience, cost, mutual respect and dignity.

The ambassador also noted that tourism generated mutual economic benefits.

“The arrival of tourists does not simply mean travellers entering a country. Hotels, restaurants, transport providers, shops, tour guides, craftspeople, public services and dozens of other sectors of the economy all benefit,” Moujani wrote.

He said travellers had also historically played an important role in building links between cultures and peoples, and sometimes in creating new opportunities for cooperation and development.

“If a new situation has emerged today, we should not view it solely as a restriction; every restriction can become an opportunity to find new paths,” the ambassador said.

Seyed Ali Moujani said there were other coastal destinations in the Black Sea region besides Georgia that could serve as alternatives for Iranian tourists.

“There are other destinations — other countries worth visiting, other cultures worth discovering and other peoples worth engaging with,” Moujani wrote.

The ambassador described Iran’s respect and friendship for Georgia and the Georgian people as unwavering, but stressed that Iran and the Iranian people’s right to choose also deserved respect.

World.title: Second chance: South Ossetia revives efforts to promote Ossetian amid leadership change
World.content:
South Ossetian Education and Science Minister Aslan Lolayev has announced plans to open a specialist class offering advanced study of the Ossetian language and literature.

Lolayev said the class would accommodate more than 30 pupils, but did not specify which school it would be based at or which year group it would be for.

“The authorities plan to open another three such classes in the next academic year — two in Tskhinvali and one in one of the districts,” Lolayev added.

He said the authorities hoped the introduction of classes offering advanced Ossetian-language study would “become one of the stages in developing a national Ossetian school system and expanding the use of the native language in education”.

Russian and Ossetian are South Ossetia’s official languages, but administrative work and education are conducted only in Russian. Russian is dominant overall, and is also the language predominantly used by the local population in everyday life.

However, Zarema Ts, a schoolteacher from Tskhinvali, says there is demand among young people for greater promotion of the Ossetian language. She believes the younger generation should therefore be encouraged to study the Ossetian language and literature, as well as Ossetian history and ethnography.

“There should be more opportunities, clubs and classes for studying Ossetian, not only within the education system but also outside educational institutions. For example, why not organise Ossetian-language classes for visitors and Russian specialists working here?”

North Ossetian experience not fully embraced

Zarema says, however, that proficiency in Ossetian is considerably higher in South Ossetia than in North Ossetia. Statistics appear to support her claim: in North Ossetia, which is part of the Russian Federation, the situation surrounding the Ossetian language has been recognised as critical, prompting the local authorities to take serious steps to preserve it.

The Alan Gymnasium, a multilingual Ossetian-Russian boarding school, has been operating in Vladikavkaz for nine years, with most subjects taught primarily in Ossetian. The school was established at the initiative of then North Ossetian leader Vyacheslav Bitarov, who continues to provide it with financial support.

South Ossetian officials, however, have been slow to adopt this model.

In early 2026, Aslan Lolayev was preparing to present a project for a national school in Tskhinvali modelled on the Alan Gymnasium. Reports said the project had already been agreed with the relevant Russian authorities and only needed to be implemented.

Lolayev was subsequently dismissed as education minister, and acting minister Rimma Pliyeva said the North Ossetian gymnasium model was unsuitable for South Ossetia. She argued that South Ossetia’s education system was already “perfectly fulfilling its role in teaching the Ossetian language”.

Second chance

Several months later, however, there was another twist: South Ossetian President Alan Gagloyev resigned early and Prime Minister Marat Kambolov took over as acting president.

Kambolov reinstated former Education Minister Aslan Lolayev, giving him another opportunity to implement at least part of his programme to expand advanced study of the Ossetian language and literature.

How successful the initiative will prove remains unclear, with South Ossetian experts so far reluctant to make predictions.

Three years ago, in September 2023, Aslan Lolayev raised concerns about a shortage of Ossetian-language textbooks.

“These textbooks cannot be purchased commercially because they were published under a state procurement programme. All copies were distributed to educational institutions. Moreover, the textbooks were published in 2019 and, if handled with care, have a lifespan of five years. After that, they need to be replaced,” he said at the time.

Lolayev added that the republication of the textbooks was included in a three-year programme that was due to be submitted to parliament and the government for consideration.

“I hope it will receive support and that we will be able to resolve this issue,” Lolayev said in 2023. There have been no reports of new textbooks since then.

South Ossetia is due to hold a presidential election on 18 September. Whether the change of leadership and the arrival of a new team, which includes Aslan Lolayev, will alter the situation remains to be seen, although there are hopes within society that it will.

Madina Valiyeva, a finalist in the Team of the Future personnel programme, for example, says that if she is appointed to an official post, one of her goals will be to establish a South Ossetian version of the Alan Gymnasium.

“There is a very apt saying: ‘No language, no nation.’ We must preserve our native language and pass it on to future generations. That is the future of our people,” Valiyeva said.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Abkhaz president voices blacksmith in cartoon
World.content:
Abkhaz President Badra Gunba has voiced a character in the animated film Nart Sasrykva, dedicated to a hero of the Abkhaz epic. Gunba provided the voice of one of the film’s characters, the blacksmith Ainar.

Work on the 36-minute animated film, which has taken five years to complete, is nearing its end, with its official premiere due in a month. Director Astamur Kvitsinia adapted the heroic epic, which has several versions, into a format designed to be engaging and accessible to children.

It is unclear why the president became involved in voicing the film. One possible explanation is the longstanding friendship between Badra Gunba and Astamur Kvitsinia, dating back to Gunba’s time as Abkhazia’s culture minister from 2011 to 2014.

Astamur Kvitsinia is widely regarded as the father of Abkhaz animation and has created more than a dozen animated films based on Abkhaz fairy tales and myths.

Versions of the Nart epic, about warrior brothers who battle giants, are found among many peoples of the Caucasus. Most scholars date the epic to the 8th-7th centuries BC.

Each people’s version has its own distinctive features and reflects its particular worldview. In the Abkhaz version, the Narts are a family of 100 brothers and their only sister. Sasrykva, the youngest of the brothers, is the epic’s main hero.

World.title: “Injustice prevails under oligarch Ivanishvili” — video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Azerbaijani “Bridge of Peace” initiative group reacts to Armenian media's biased position
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 14. The "Peace Bridge" Initiative Group on Azerbaijan has expressed deep disappointment regarding the biased attitude of Armenian media and the unacceptable tone of public discussions concerning the visit of the diplomatic corps to the Karabakh and East Zangezur regions of Azerbaijan on September 11–12, 2026.

Trend presents the statement issued by the group regarding this matter.

"The Azerbaijani 'Bridge of Peace' initiative group expresses deep disappointment regarding the hostile media reaction and the unacceptable tone of public discourse in Armenia concerning the visit of the diplomatic corps to the Karabakh and East Zangezur regions of Azerbaijan on September 11–12, 2026.

First and foremost, the visit of the diplomatic corps to the sovereign territory of Azerbaijan should not, in itself, be a subject of dispute. In particular, verbal attacks directed at ambassadors and countries for participating in such a visit are concerning and contradict the fact that Armenia recognizes Azerbaijan's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Azerbaijan and Armenia are currently in a post-conflict period, and both countries face the complex task of overcoming decades of confrontation. As representatives of civil society, and with the support of the governments of Azerbaijan and Armenia, we are taking steps—within the framework of peace initiatives—to facilitate the peace process, encourage dialogue, and support confidence-building measures.

Cultural heritage within the territory of Azerbaijan belongs to the Azerbaijani people and is protected by the state.

To ensure fairness, issues regarding cultural heritage must be discussed on the basis of reciprocity and open dialogue. To advance these goals, civil society representatives have established a platform for professional discussion of issues that form an integral part of the peace process agenda between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

The peace process must not be allowed to come under pressure from revanchist forces, as this would seriously jeopardize further progress toward peace. We call upon Armenian society to demonstrate a responsible approach to this issue and not to succumb to the provocations of those harboring malicious intent, whether in Armenia, as well as beyond its borders.

Farhad Mammadov

Kamala Mammadova

Rusif Huseynov

Dilyara Afandiyeva

Ramil Iskandarli,” the statement said.

World.title: Trump post-wedding festivities paid for by Russian businessman, couple confirms
World.content:
Donald Trump Jr's new wife, Bettina, has confirmed her May wedding weekend celebration was partially funded by a man with close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In a post on her Instagram page on Monday, Bettina Trump wrote that the man, Umar Kremlev, was a "dear friend," who "very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding".

The post was signed by the couple.

Trump skips son's wedding US President Donald Trump misses his son's wedding ceremony in the Bahamas, citing his "love of the United States" as a key reason to stay in Washington.

"It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful," it read.

ProPublica, a non-profit investigative website, reported earlier on Monday that the wedding between Donald Trump Jr and socialite Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas was heavily funded by Mr Kremlev, a Russian oligarch who heads the International Boxing Association.

ProPublica reported that Mr Kremlev "footed the bill for hundreds of thousands of dollars of wedding expenses", including paying to rent out one of two private islands where the three-day party was held and a fireworks show.

In the post, Bettina Trump said that she and the president's son were married in a private ceremony "surrounded ONLY by our family".

"The weekend that followed had actually been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends. It was never intended to be our wedding weekend. When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds.

"It's unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from.

" Friendship doesn't require a political motive. Generosity doesn't automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift. "

Mr Kremlev was recently honoured with the Order of Friendship by Mr Putin, according to the International Boxing Association, and accompanied Mr Putin to China as part of a Russian delegation, according to the Chinese state media cited by the outlet.

US President Donald Trump missed his son's wedding ceremony in May, citing his "love of the United States" as a key reason to stay in Washington.

"While I very much wanted to be with my son, Don Jr., and the newest member of the Trump Family, his soon to be wife, Bettina, circumstances pertaining to Government, and my love for the United States of America, do not allow me to do so," he said in a Truth Social post.

"Congratulations to Don and Bettina!" he wrote.

AP

World.title: Country pride events struggle to survive as volunteers dwindle
World.content:
Organisers of queer festivals in regional Western Australia say their events are at risk of vanishing due to a lack of people willing to help coordinate every year, as another Pride parade bites the dust.

In Carnarvon, about 900 kilometres north of Perth, those pressures have brought the town's 2026 parade to an end after three years, despite being well supported in the community.

Most of the committee behind Queernarvon has stepped down or moved away, leaving the group without enough volunteers.

More than 300 people attended the first year of Queernarvon events. (Supplied: Andrew Robertson)

In the state's south, Busselton's long-running Pride parade has also been cancelled, with organisers instead directing their limited resources towards education and wellbeing events.

But in the Pilbara, a Pride festival that began as a small games night among friends has grown to attract about 1,500 people, with organisers crediting support from the wider community for its success.

So, what are the obstacles for LGTBIQA+ people living in the regions?

Changing views

Queernarvon chair Carmen Reilly said Pride events played an important role in regional communities.

In her view, there had been a shift in public perception towards trans, gender diverse and young LGBTQI+ people.

Carmen Reilly (right) says pride events help to connect people. (Supplied: Andrew Robertson)

"I have had several conversations over the last few months with people who have never met a trans person, but have seen posts and AI clips on social media and have formed their opinions," she said.

"I say to those people, 'If you're basing your opinions and ideas on social media, put the phone down, go out and meet someone who has a different life experience to you.'"

She said events such as these helped build real connections within communities.

"There's more connecting us than dividing us," she said.

Finding a community

Johnathan Trace, who is working in Carnarvon on a holiday visa, said he made the decision to leave his home country of the United States because the rise of the far right made him feel unsafe as a trans man.

"I was like, 'It's time. I need to get out of here,'" he said.

Johnathan Trace says people like him are having to carry a huge mental load with the rise of the far right around the world. (ABC Pilbara: Rachel Hagan)

Since being in Australia, Mr Trace said he had felt safer but still experienced moments that made him feel unsafe and unwelcome.

Those ranged from nasty comments delivered by strangers in the bathroom, to homophobic outbursts from customers he was serving at work.

Mr Trace said it was a shame the Carnarvon event was cancelled, as there were a lack of spaces to discuss his life experiences as a trans man.

"You're surrounded by all these backpackers who are just here for a good time, who don't want to talk about politics or anything that ruins their good vibes," Mr Trace said.

" It's very hard to find a real community where you can talk about your queerness and the negative things you face with that. "

Johnathan Trace has travelled across the world to find a community that accepts him living as himself. (ABC Pilbara: Rachel Hagan)

Mining towns lead the way

A bright spot for WA Pride celebrations is in the state's mining region.

The Pilbara Pride Festival started from a small games night among friends, but is now in its fifth year, with about 1,500 people estimated to attend the events across places such as Port Hedland, Karratha and Onslow.

PHLAGS+ runs events across the region for the Pilbara Pride Festival. (Supplied)

Port Hedland Lesbian, Allies, Gays Society (PHLAGS+) secretary Gloria Jacob put the success down to dedicated volunteers and support from local government and the resources sector.

"This year in particular, the one thing that filled my cup was the high school students asking us to hold a workshop at the school, and the high school allowing us to do that," Ms Jacob said.

But she said it had not always been this way.

"I can tell you there were times in the early days where it wasn't that pleasant, and it still isn't pleasant," she said.

" But the main reason we do it is to ensure our young people, our First Nations people and those who are less able to access these safe spaces know PHLAGS+ exist. "

'Space to be themselves'

A local church initially protested against the PHLAGS+ Pride events.

"But the second year they actually marched with us in the parade," Ms Jacob said.

"The more people engage and the more people become aware — it becomes the norm."

Pride events in regional areas attracted visitors from across the state. (Supplied: Andrew Robertson)

Ms Jacob said if support was not upheld by the wider community, the regions will lose their diversity.

"If they don't feel like they are welcome or supported or have space to be themselves openly, you're going to lose them to the city," she said.

"The city can be brought to the communities, we've proven it through Pilbara Pride."

World.title: NSW Police investigating after 13yo Muslim girl verbally abused on bus
World.content:
"Immigrant mutt … You don't deserve to be here," a stranger on a bus said to 13-year-old Janna last week, according to footage that has gone viral online.

Janna, who was wearing a hijab and her school uniform, was riding the bus back from school in Sydney when the incident occurred.

Warning: This story contains details that may be distressing for some readers.

"I kept telling him I was born here in Australia. I have never left," Janna told the ABC.

In a video recording seen by the ABC, the accused man can be heard calling Janna names, including a "c**k sucking f***ing animal", an "immigrant dog", "a f***ing terrorist" and "a piece of sh**".

Janna said she did not know who the man was, and kept reminding him of her young age, but said the derogatory comments continued.

"It felt really … disgusting," she said.

Sydney student Janna, 13, says she was subject to a racial attack on a bus. She is pictured with her mother Roula. (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

According to Janna, the verbal abuse started after she saw the man taking photos of another young girl on the bus wearing a hijab, without her knowledge.

Janna stood up for the girl and told her what was happening, which she said then triggered the tirade caught on video.

A witness on the bus filmed the incident and uploaded it to her social media account with the caption: "I'm so f***ing scared."

The video has since gone viral with thousands of shares.

Janna says she did not expect the tirade to continue as it did. (Supplied)

'Not the worst of them' Islamophobia attacks on the rise

In another video of the incident seen by the ABC, the man was seen arguing back and forth with another woman before saying: "I can't wait until they kill all of you", appearing to direct his comments to the Muslim women on the bus.

After the incident, Janna and her mother Roula filed a police report with NSW Police, who told the ABC that "inquiries into the incident are continuing".

NSW Police acting deputy commissioner Peter McKenna described the alleged conduct as "disgusting".

"We will investigate that matter, and we will throw the book at that person when we find them because it is outrageous," he told 702 ABC Sydney.

"Social cohesion at the moment is at a precipice, especially since [the terror attack at] Bondi."

Transport for NSW has been contacted for comment.

This case is part of a growing number of anti-Muslim incidents recorded by the Islamophobia Register Australia (IRA).

The Register said reported incidents had increased 612 per cent since October 2023, according to their research.

Aishah Ali said bystanders should call out Islamophobia as they see it. (ABC News: Simon Amery )

IRA's executive director, Aishah Ali, who learned of the Sydney bus incident after it was reported to the Register, said she was "beyond horrified".

"Janna's incident was not a salient one," Ms Ali said.

"We have reports like this that come in every other day. We have victims who are experiencing verbal abuse daily.

" This situation actually is extreme, but it's actually not the worst of them. "

Women and children have increasingly become targets of anti-Muslim hate, Ms Ali said.

"Women have historically, through all of our documented research, disproportionately been affected by Islamophobia," she said.

More than 90 per cent of targets of Islamophobia are Muslim women, according to Ms Ali.

"These experiences are normalised by the public and are now also being normalised as part and parcel of just being a Muslim Australian," she said.

Intervention to tackle hate

Roula says she is proud of her daughter's response. (ABC News)

Janna's mother Roula said she was "incredibly proud" of her daughter for standing up for the other girl.

"The way she responded, the way she respected her environment and her hijab. It shows her character.

"She stood strong and said I'm not going to tolerate that," she said.

Roula said she had taught her daughter to be vigilant about possible Islamophobia when Janna began wearing a hijab earlier this year.

"When she told me what happened, I told her, 'Janna, you're going to go through a lot of that as a hijabi'," she said/

Muslim man attacked on way to mosque A Muslim man has escaped a near-miss knife attack on his way to evening prayers after police say he was set upon by two men metres away from his local mosque.

Roula said she was horrified that her daughter had very little support from others on the bus.

"Nobody intervened — I was not expecting the passengers to intervene, but the bus driver should have stopped the bus," she said.

Ms Ali said bystander intervention was key to combating Islamophobia.

"It should never be on a 13-year-old to have to take up space in that sort of way and put them in a position of unsafety," she said.

"Especially where it's verbal abuse, and there's a young victim; it should never be on a young girl."

World.title: Ella Heads cops big ban for bump that broke star Demon's jaw
World.content:
Port Adelaide defender Ella Heads has been handed a three-match AFLW ban for her bump that fractured the jaw of Melbourne's Eliza McNamara.

McNamara had just fired off a handball in Sunday's 51-point win when Heads ran in and collected the midfielder front-on with her shoulder.

A dazed McNamara had blood coming out from her face as she was assisted from the ground.

The 24-year-old was taken to hospital, with the Demons confirming on Monday she had undergone surgery, with no timeline set for her return.

The incident was classified as careless conduct, severe impact and high contact, drawing a three-match ban.

"That was a really poor challenge," former AFLW star Kate McCarthy said.

"It was probably one of the worst bumps I’ve seen on the AFLW field in regards to being late, being high and just being really careless and not eliciting that duty of care that we now know is placed on you as an AFLW player when you elect to bump."

That equates to a quarter of the 12-round home-and-away season, and Heads will miss games against Sydney, the Western Bulldogs and Adelaide unless Port can downgrade the charge.

In other tribunal news, West Coast's Abbygail Bushby was handed a one-match ban for her clumsy collision with the Brisbane Lions' Sophie Peters.

Peters had her head over the ball when Bushby ran in and tumbled over her opponent.

Richmond's Montana McKinnon was handed a one-match rough conduct ban for her run-in with St Kilda's Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: 'Never wanted to be that pest': Slain paramedic's father not giving up
World.content:
Surrounded by friends and strangers dressed in his son's favourite colour, Jeff Tougher looked anything but alone.

Woonona Bowling Club was filled with laughter, prizes and people determined to support the family of paramedic Steven Tougher, who was fatally stabbed while on a work break in Sydney's south-west on April 14, 2023.

The crowd at the Woonona Bowling Club for the fundraiser on September 11. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Jeff joked with the crowd, while his wife, Jill, said the fundraiser would have suited their son perfectly.

"I just want everyone to know that Stevie was so much more than what happened to him on the 14th of April," she said.

"This is right up his alley; a big party, everyone having fun and still helping the community."

Paramedic Steven Tougher was fatally stabbed in April 2023. (Supplied)

But away from the crowds, Jeff worries whether he is doing enough to honour his son's legacy.

"The three o'clock in the morning waking up thinking, 'Am I doing the right thing? Am I representing my son in the proper way?'" he said.

"Have I upset somebody? Have I said something that has damaged my chances? Have I offended a politician? Am I that pest? I never wanted to be that pest."

Following Steven's death, Jeff found himself becoming an unlikely advocate for frontline-worker safety.

The family remains determined to secure legislative change recognising Steven's legacy. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

During visits to ambulance stations and a road trip distributing Steven's Law stickers, he says he and Jill spoke with more than 1,000 paramedics.

The warm welcomes often gave way to quieter disclosures.

"When the fanfare died down and we'd been there a little while, they'd start to pull you aside and say, 'I need to talk to you about this. This is what happened to me and I'm not being supported,'" Jeff said.

" They'd say, 'We're told to just suck it up. It's part of the job.' "

Jill and Jeff have spoken to more than a thousand paramedics around the state about their experiences. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

NSW Ambulance figures show 1,500 incidents of occupational violence were reported against staff in the first eight months of 2026.

There were 1,376 reported incidents throughout 2025 and 1,081 in 2024.

Occupational violence covers a broad range of behaviour, including physical assault, intimidation, threats, verbal abuse, inappropriate touching and sexualised behaviour.

NSW Ambulance said this year's apparent increase could partly be attributed to a change introduced in January requiring emergency medical call-takers to record any aggressive behaviour from patients or callers.

Jeff said hearing paramedics' experiences had given him a new understanding of the cumulative effect of violence and abuse.

He said repeated incidents could cause psychological harm and lead highly trained clinicians to question whether they wanted to remain in the profession.

"These people study for years," he said.

" It's all about service to the community, service to others. Steven was going to be a paramedic regardless. He'd do it for free if he could. "

NSW Ambulance said it supported and encouraged staff to report violence and aggression, and paramedics had its full backing not to enter or to withdraw from situations they considered unsafe.

It said it had established a dedicated occupational violence prevention team, expanded face-to-face safety training and improved the way incidents are reported, categorised and reviewed.

The service is also improving mobile duress technology and working with NSW Police on information-sharing.

A spokesperson said the Tougher family would always have the "unwavering support" of NSW Ambulance.

From anger to advocacy

Jeff's advocacy began in the immediate aftermath of his son's death.

"I remember when grief turned to anger and I remember when grief turned to vengeance," he said.

"I remember saying to myself, 'You're not going to get anywhere harbouring those thoughts and wasting energy on those emotions.'

"I thought to myself, 'What can I do to help my son achieve a legacy for what he sacrificed that day?'"

The answer came to him almost immediately: Steven's Law.

Jeff and Jill Tougher have become tireless advocates for frontline workers since Steven's death in 2023. (Facebook: Steven Tougher)

Jeff initially called for a mandatory 12-month prison sentence for anyone convicted of assaulting a frontline worker.

He also sought body-worn cameras, access to stab or slash-resistant garments and a major public awareness campaign intended to make Steven's Law widely understood.

But the NSW government does not support mandatory minimum sentences, arguing they remove judicial discretion and risk producing unjust outcomes.

"Courts must be able to impose appropriate sentences based on the facts and circumstances of each case," a government spokesperson said.

Jeff has not abandoned the campaign, but he has begun looking for a compromise.

He has suggested a mandatory $1,000 fine as a possible starting point and now describes Steven's Law as a package of prevention, protection, consequences and public education rather than a single penalty.

"I was starting the negotiations at the 12-month mandatory jail term," he said.

" Let's work back. Let's work back to something we can put together. You can't just flick it. "

The man who killed Steven, Jordan Fineanganofo, admitted carrying out the fatal attack, but in 2024 the NSW Supreme Court found him not criminally responsible because of a mental health impairment.

The court accepted he was acutely psychotic and unable to understand that his actions were wrong.

Family members of Steven Tougher embrace outside the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney. (AAP: Duncan Murray)

He was detained as a forensic patient and remains subject to review by the NSW Mental Health Review Tribunal.

Jeff has also questioned whether failures in the mental health system allowed Fineanganofo's condition to deteriorate before the attack.

Frontline offence penalties

NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research data shows 507 charges under laws covering offences against frontline emergency and health workers were finalised in the year to March 2026.

The offences range from hindering, harassment and intimidation to assault causing injury and are not limited to incidents involving paramedics.

Of 172 proven court appearances where an offence against a frontline worker attracted the most serious penalty, 42 resulted in custody.

Supervised community sentences were the most common outcome, imposed in 65 cases.

Separately, 91 of the 507 finalised charges were dismissed because of mental illness or cognitive impairment.

Fines were imposed in 17 of the proven principal-offence matters, averaging $750 for emergency worker offences and $981 for health worker offences.

In 2023, the Sydney Opera House sails were illuminated in memory of Steven Tougher. (AAP: Steven Saphore)

The NSW government said it had worked closely with Steven's parents and introduced several changes following his death.

It increased the maximum penalty for knife possession to four years in prison, prohibited knife sales to 16- and 17-year-olds and introduced legislation to make its knife wanding powers permanent.

The government said the reforms had led to more knife prosecutions and an increase in custodial sentences for knife possession.

It also pointed to the 25-year standard non-parole period for murdering an emergency worker.

Campaign continues

Other measures sought by Jeff remain under consideration or incomplete.

NSW Ambulance has trialled body-worn cameras, but a broader introduction remains subject to consultation with the workforce.

The service said it had also committed to completing independent Charles Sturt University research into the effectiveness of stab-resistant garments.

Health Minister Ryan Park announced the NSW government would kick-start the foundation with a $17,500 donation at the fundraiser. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

More than three years after Steven's death, Jeff remains frustrated by the pace of the response.

He wants the premier, attorney-general, relevant ministers, NSW Ambulance and unions to meet and determine what could form part of Steven's Law.

"All I'm asking from the government is that we all sit down in one room and come up with something that we can call Steven's Law," he said.

"I don't think that's a lot to ask."

Jeff said the campaign had consumed his retirement and placed pressure on his relationship with Jill, as each member of the family experienced grief differently.

"It's very taxing and it puts strain on your marriage, there's no question about it," he said.

"Grief works in different stages. Grief takes different time for different people."

But at Woonona Bowling Club, the campaign's more joyful direction was on display.

The fundraiser supported nursing and paramedicine scholarships and a foundation established in Steven's name.

Jill and Jeff Tougher's relationship has been strained by their grief and the campaign for reform. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

Asked what Steven would think of the campaign, the foundation, scholarships and the crowd wearing yellow in his honour, Jeff paused.

"He'd be embarrassed, to start with," he said.

"But he'd be proud."

World.title: Live: Emmy Awards 2026 live: Mariska Hargitay opens as Hacks and Widow's Bay fight for Best Comedy
World.content:
Look, I've got nothing against Hacks, and I understand the impulse to want the show to get a big emotional award for its last season, but Widow's Bay is simply the best show to debut in the past 12 months, and here's why.

Creator Katie Dippold is the person who posted the Babadook at the adult wine party tweet.

But if you need even more evidence...

Slipping onto Apple TV in April with nary a peep, Widow's Bay is like if you layered together a misty Stephen King novel, Mike Flanagan's Haunting of Hill House and the best seasons of Parks and Rec into a cake that is somehow more delicious than the sum of its parts.

Matthew Rhys as a flopsweaty mayor trying to turn a clearly haunted town into the "next Martha's Vineyard"! Katie O'Flynn as Patricia, a never-before-seen type of final girl! Stephen Root as the town kook who's actually right!

It is extremely rare for a show (or a movie) to be able to balance comedy and horror without detracting from each other, yet Widow's Bay is hilarious and terrifying in perfectly equal measures.

Here's hoping I get to pull out Patricia's dance moves when Widow's Bay is named Best Comedy.

World.title: Riverland men casting aside tools and tractors to work in disability
World.content:
When Brody Thompson finished school and began thinking about his future, a career in the disability caring field was never something he had considered.

But after a few years working on his family farm, the then-24-year-old decided he needed a change of pace.

"[I was] just really stuck in a rut. Eight hours a day sitting in the tractor; it's the same view all day, not a lot changes," Mr Thompson said.

Brody says he felt "stuck in a rut" working on his family farm after finishing school. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

" I just needed a little bit of variety in my life. "

When a friend from his local football club, in South Australia's Riverland, suggested he consider applying for a job in disability support, Mr Thompson decided he had nothing to lose.

He is now among more than a dozen men making up half the workforce of a local NDIS provider that mentors and supports children and young adults across the community and wider Riverland area.

He is also part of a changing workforce with more men taking up the career.

Mr Thompson said while the shift from the farm to disability support work had been dramatic, he had not looked back.

Brody's workplace has more than a dozen other male support workers and administration staff. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

"I'd say there definitely was a stigma [around working in disability] for me," he said.

"[I thought] you're in-house just caring all the time, you're getting people up out of bed, toileting and showering them. I do a bit of that [but] there's so much more to it.

"Once you're all in, you realise how much need there is and how much you can help. There's nothing more rewarding than helping."

Max Hall is a part-time client of Mr Thompson's, who also shares his time with fellow carer, Harry Papageorgios.

Mr Hall said he appreciated the opportunity to engage with male role models with similar interests, including AFL.

One of Brody's clients Max Hall (left) says he likes doing physical activity during their sessions. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

"Harry, he's a good man. Brody, I know he goes for Hawthorn, [which is] 'hawful' actually," the 20-year-old Adelaide Crows supporter said with a grin.

"[But] it has made me happy a lot."

The job that 'changed my life'

Loxton-based disability worker Haiden Button said there was still a negative stigma related to support work, but it had slowly decreased in recent years.

The 32-year-old had spent more than a decade working as a crash repairer after completing his apprenticeship while still a teenager.

Loxton's Haiden Button came into disability work after more than a decade in a trade. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

Six years ago, after Mr Button recognised the toll the work was taking on his health, he left the trade that he felt defined his identity.

He said a shift to disability support work had given him a renewed sense of purpose.

"Without making it sound too dramatic, changing to disability support work has changed my life for the better," Mr Button said.

"I didn't quite realise how maybe unhealthy my mental health was, and also just my wellbeing, until starting something where I was happy to come to work every day.

Haiden says there has not been a day when he isn't happy to come to work. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

"There's been challenging days for sure, but none where I wouldn't want to be here."

Rising trend at a national level

National data suggests that across the past 10 years, more men are choosing to work in disability support.

Brody Thompson and his fellow male support workers have built up a strong relationship with their client base. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

The National Disability Services' (NDS) 2024-25 workforce census survey was completed by more than 60,000 disability support workers.

The data showed the caring sector was still dominated by women, with 61 per cent of participants female.

However, NDS director of policy and advocacy Karen Stace said men in the workforce had risen from 29 per cent in 2015 to 33 per cent in 2025.

Karen Stace from the NDS says the number of men working in disability has grown over the past decade. (Supplied: National Disability Services)

"It's positive to see more men choosing disability support as a career," Ms Stace said.

"The bigger opportunity is ensuring the sector is able to invest in attracting and retaining a diverse, skilled workforce so people with disability can access high-quality support wherever they live."

The rise in men in the disability support industry came at the same time as National Centre for Vocational Education Research data revealed there had been a decline in Australians finishing apprenticeships and traineeships.

A fulfilling and active career

For Mr Thompson and Mr Button, ditching the tools and the tractor had not only given them a rewarding career, but it had also given them an active and fun outlet.

Mr Thompson said his sessions with clients revolved around physical activity like sport and gym sessions, while Mr Button said his involved a lot of ground maintenance work.

Haiden still has a very physical side to his new career. (ABC Riverland: Oliver Brown)

"Hundred per cent [I enjoy my job] for the clients, the interactions and helping our supported staff to enjoy their roles and have a sense that they're contributing to the community," Mr Button said.

"As well as that, I still get to go out and work with my hands.

"We do a lot of grounds maintenance and all sorts of other jobs outside, as well as all our workshop jobs."

World.title: Fitzroy Crossing calls for stronger FASD support
World.content:
Aboriginal leaders in Western Australia's far north are calling for greater government support for fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD), as local schoolchildren march to raise awareness.

The calls for FASD treatment support come seven years after a coronial inquest into the deaths of 13 children.

Warning: This story contains references to suicide and self-harm.

FASD is a permanent neurodevelopmental condition that occurs when a fetus is exposed to alcohol in the womb, often leaving children struggling with learning, impulsivity and understanding consequences.

A 2019 coronial inquest into the deaths of 13 children and young people over a four-year period in the Kimberley examined factors that made them vulnerable to suicide, including possible neurodevelopmental impairment.

Coroner Ros Fogliani found circumstantial evidence FASD played a role in some of the deaths and recommended increased government funding for FASD prevention, diagnosis and treatment.

However, seven years on, Marninwarntikura Women's Resource Centre (MWRC) chief executive and Gooniyandi, Kija woman Emily Carter said many of the coronial recommendations remained unfulfilled.

"The recommendations have never really been implemented by the government at all," she said.

'Fighting for our children'

Last week, more than 200 people marched through Fitzroy Crossing, 2,600 kilometres north of Perth, waving banners for International FASD Awareness Day.

Marninwarntikura Women's Resource Centre chief executive Emily Carter addresses the crowd at the FASD Awareness Day march in Fitzroy Crossing. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark)

Ms Carter said the community had been fighting for better support for children and families for decades.

"We are a very strong community, and we're fighting for supports for our children and their families every day," she said.

The 2010 Lililwan study, completed by MWRC and Nindilingarri Cultural Health Services (NCHS), found one in five Fitzroy Valley children had FASD, among the highest rates globally.

NCHS senior support officer Ishmael Croft said inadequate support could leave young people with FASD especially vulnerable if they encountered the justice system.

Nindilingarri Cultural Health Services senior support worker Ishmael Croft addresses the crowd at the FASD march in Fitzroy Crossing. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark )

He also cited a 2018 study at WA's Banksia Hill Detention Centre, showing more than a third of assessed children had FASD.

Call for early diagnosis

WA Children's Court president Hylton Quail last week told ABC Perth access to FASD assessments in the Kimberley was crucial for children before the court.

"The big problem we have is I cannot get the necessary specialists to do assessments, let alone treatment, north of Perth," he said.

"We do not have enough psychiatrists and paediatricians working in the childhood space to do this work."

More than 200 people carried FASD awareness banners down the streets of Fitzroy Crossing for the annual march. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark )

MWRC strategic priority lead Sue Thomas said waiting until a child entered the justice system overlooked the need for earlier support.

"If we are looking at the impact of an assessment on sentencing, it's too late," she said.

Coinciding with the march, MWRC launched a culturally safe FASD health resources program.

"No person goes out to deliberately harm their unborn child," Ms Carter said.

"But we also know for women things have happened in their lives, whether it is domestic violence, or homelessness.

"We have trauma-informed resources to fully understand how trauma has and continues to impact our families and children."

Colourful banners painted with FASD awareness slogans line the streets of Fitzroy Crossing for this year's annual march. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark )

Government defends FASD response

A state government spokesperson said it had responded to the coroner's inquest with educational, health and social programs.

"Schools across the Kimberley are also working with families and local organisations to improve engagement and attendance for primary school students, including those affected by FASD," they said.

"This includes On Country learning programs, support from school psychologists, and access to specialist FASD training and resources to help staff better understand how FASD can affect a child's learning, behaviour and engagement at school."

Sergeant Jody Worthington helps a youngster along during the FASD march. (ABC Kimberley: Natasha Clark )

The spokesperson highlighted a progress report on the coronial findings would be released later this year, "providing a further update on the implementation of the recommendations".

World.title: ‘Certificate 3 in prostitution’: Teacher demoted and moved schools over comments
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland courts ‘Certificate 3 in prostitution’: Teacher demoted and moved schools over comments Julius Dennis September 15, 2026 — 10:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The head of a department at a Queensland school has lost his appeal of a decision to demote him and force him to change schools over a series of creepy comments he was found by the industrial relations commission to have made to female students, including that one could have a “Certificate 3 in prostitution”. Scott Alan Barnard also discussed his own nipple piercings, greek statues with erect penises, and told a student he was “glad it’s your butt warmth that I’m sitting in”. The comments were made at various times in 2023 and 2024 to year 11 and 12 students at an undisclosed state school, who said he told he had drawn other students naked, and found it strange there were less pregnant students now than when he was in school. A teacher has lost his appeal of a decision to demote him over inappropriate remarks. Phil Carrick According to the ruling, which he appealed to the Queensland Industrial Relations Commission (QIRC) earlier this year, he made further comments of a sexual nature to a Year 11 student in 2023.



The names of the students and the school Barnard taught at have been suppressed. “When ... student O sought your assistance with positioning paper for printing, you stated words to the effect that you thought as a girl she would ‘know plenty of positions’. Student O interpreted this to mean ‘sex positions’ and it caused her to feel uncomfortable and embarrassed,” it said. He also told another student she had nice lips, and asked students to locate some “faggots”, which he said meant sticks, not the derogatory slur for LGBTQIA+ persons. Barnard, who had been working for the education department since 2005, denied the conversations about the greek statues, making nude artworks, and the “positions” and prostitution comments. According to the ruling, Barnard had received a sexual harassment complaint in March 2024, and an internal investigation found he should be disciplined for the allegation he had engaged in inappropriate and unprofessional manner towards students, which he denied.



Barnard had not been formally disciplined before, but had been subject to management action in 2023 after he made inappropriate remarks about a student’s physique, and said, “why go to the strip club when you can go to the beach and women are practically naked anyway”, the previous year. In his appeal, Barnard argued he could not travel 50 minutes to his new school as he was the carer of a child with a disability, and he would have to teach outside his expertise. Commissioner Peter O’Neill refused the appeal, telling Barnard he should have raised the issue of his caring for the child during the show cause process, and he had waited too long to launch his appeal. The disciplinary decision was made in December, and took effect in March 2026, after which Barnard had 21 days to appeal the decision, but did not do so until April. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant ‘M’ evidence to resume after court hears former 2GB broadcaster bought flowers weekly for former athlete
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent relating to six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the alleged physical acts occurred.

Jones, pictured on Monday, is standing trial on 22 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. Steven Siewert

Yesterday, the third of the six complainants, a former athlete dubbed “M”, started giving evidence.

“M” returns to the witness box today. Yesterday, he told the court:

Jones kissed him on the corner of his mouth at an event in Sydney about a decade ago. “I think I froze at that time,” “M” said.

The court heard Jones texted him that night: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after, had to go back to work. You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

“M” replied: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now; thanks mate xoxo.” The conversation ended in “M” saying “let me know when we can catch up. Lots of love” and Jones replying: “I will darling. Big kisses forever.”

The court heard that Jones texted “M” on another occasion, after receiving a photo: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up darling [name] xxx”. “M” said he did not respond immediately. Hours later, Jones wrote: “I hope my message did not upset you. I love you.” The man said he responded the next day, writing: “Not at all mate. It’s nice to be loved.”

The complainant said he had used the word “mate” for many reasons. “I know I’d made it very clear that ... it wasn’t moving into a relationship, so ‘mate’ was my way of pushing back, I guess.”

“M” said that on the last occasion he visited Jones at his harbourside apartment, the broadcaster kissed him repeatedly on the cheek towards his lips and said words to the effect of, “I love you so much, you don’t know how much I love you.” The complainant said he could feel Jones’ genitals on his leg .

The complainant said he pushed the broadcaster away and said, “OK, mate”, in a tone intended to convey “get away from me”, and “got out of there as quickly as possible”.

The court heard Jones had sent the complainant gifts including weekly flowers for years and a dinner set. The complainant agreed he also sent Jones flowers at least once.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Frank, fearless, but not so free-style? Staff survey changes raise eyebrows
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service Frank, fearless, but not so free-style? Staff survey changes raise eyebrows Matt Dennien Updated September 15, 2026 — 10:05am ,first published September 14, 2026 — 7:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: a Working for Queensland survey prompt, “vacancy management” hits Child Safety, and wage ruling saga lands senior teachers on par with their juniors. It’s everyone’s favourite time of the year. No, not the seasonal change of spring – Working for Queensland survey month! By everyone, of course, we mean those with thoughts about their public sector employment they would maybe only dare lay out in the free-text general feedback box of the anonymised questionnaire. This year, however, it seems there could be a catch. Queensland public service HQ at One William Street. Matt Dennien Word has reached the Circus tent from multiple agencies the no-holds-barred rant box has disappeared from some surveys, or been replaced with a more restrictive prompt for others.



Since landing in inboxes from late August, some eager (only about 20 per cent of the 330,0000-strong workforce filled it out in 2025) and eagle-eyed public servants have clocked the curious changes. But it’s not uniform across the sector, with the separately collected free-text section included at the discretion of each agency and sent directly, unedited, to the boss. We’ve caught whispers some folks receiving surveys have this year found no open feedback section at the end. Other departments we’ve had intel from are said to have replaced the general feedback prompt with one asking what you’d tell someone considering a job there, or what is one thing you would change.



“It’s not as open-ended as it has been in previous years,” a department source said, speaking to us on condition of anonymity for perhaps the obvious reason of not being authorised to do so. Related Article Public service Returning kindness: The volunteers who emotionally rejuvenate Roma Street’s police They noted it seemed to be an attempt to steer staff away from airing more detailed or specific gripes. One former agency chief, also granted anonymity, told us they viewed it as one of the most important parts of the surveys because of the freeing, anonymised nature of the comments. They suggested any removal of or constraining of this would reflect a lack of willingness to “really hear what people think”.



With a couple of weeks left to complete, we imagine more will discover the changes as they open them closer to the due date – a practice Circus members are certainly not immune from on our workplace feedback forms, either. But what to do if you discover you’re cut off from the trauma dump you were hoping to give, or have already been confronted by such an injustice? We’ve got you covered. Fill out the form below (on a non-work device and network) and tell us instead. Drop contact details if you’re willing to talk more, anonymously, of course. We’ll even try and publish what we can in a future segment. Let the frank and fearless feedback flow!



‘Vacancy management’ comes for Child Safety frontline support roles Fresh on the heels of the state’s first credit rating downgrade in almost 20-years, Circus can add a seventh department to its list of those with various efforts in place to squeeze staffing budgets. The latest “vacancy management strategy” word (don’t call it a hiring freeze!) is from over at Belinda Drew’s Department of Families, Seniors, Disability Services and Child Safety. There, the strategy is said to review vacant roles across child safety, disability services and corporate support before they can be filled. Those not deemed “key frontline” require stricter approval. This includes sign-off by a deputy director-general and a documented rationale. So far, so similar to what we’ve heard from widely across the sector.



But the thing that has some child safety staff, and their union (Together), up in arms? What, exactly, is being classified as a frontline role under the exemption list. In particular, the lack of an exemption for administration and business officers in child safety service centres – who keep such centres, which support frontline child protection workers, running. “These roles are critical to frontline child protections, and they should be treated as critical workers when it comes time to fill them,” Together assistant secretary Dee Spink said in a statement. “The department says this isn’t a recruitment freeze, but for some workers it can feel like one.”



A department spokesperson said vacancy management was just one part of efforts to balance the books and ensure focus on its priorities, with all efforts to fill vacancies reviewed against workforce needs. For what it’s worth, we quizzed independent economist Saul Eslake about this vacancy management approach to belt-tightening while chatting to him on Friday about that credit downgrade. His view? “They’re a lazy way of trying to save money,” Eslake offered. “They’re fairly crude measures and not ones that I would ever support.” Eslake also reckoned the roughly 3 per cent staff expense growth projected from next financial year in Treasurer David Janetzki’s June budget (this year’s is 5.4 per cent) is only possible with a proper freeze on the size of the public service. Either that, or that slim surplus pencilled in for after the 2028 election might end up being kicked down the road – something we’re sure the ratings agencies will be watching closely.





The first band of this classification is available to those with two or more years of satisfactory service as a “senior teacher”. The second, EST 2, can be reached after three years at EST 1. That higher band was created in the 2019 agreement and is not reflected in the award. While EST 1 wages were set to lift through a safety net tied to the state wage case ruling, EST 2 wages were not. Then acting general secretary Brendan Crotty said the union clocked the issue weeks ago, raising it with Sharon Schimming’s apparently unaware department and Minister John-Paul Langbroek. Eventually, a departmental directive was issued to allow EST 2 teachers to get the higher award rate. This temporary fix, however, essentially leaves more senior teachers on an equal pay rate to those on a lower band until the difference can be sorted via the broader ongoing arbitration process. Yikes.



The issue has, as you might imagine, gone down like a tonne of lead pencils for teachers – some of whom have taken to the union’s social media comment sections to give an unfavourable report card of even some of the union process. Queensland teachers gather in Queen’s Park during the second of two Queensland Teachers’ Union strike days last year. Polina Levina/Getty Images “The QTU acknowledges that some members at EST 2 level may understandably feel frustrated that, for the time being, this means being paid at the same, if higher, rate as EST 1,” Crotty wrote to members last week. That “time being” is likely to still be some time yet, given arbitration hearings before the Queensland Industrial Relations Commission have now been given a start date of… April 6 next year. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email on m.dennien@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. World.title: Why you should think twice before complaining on your next cruise
World.content:
Reviews & adviceCruises Why you should think twice before complaining on your next cruise Brian Johnston September 15, 2026 — 9:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I could name a dozen people who’ve had a significant influence on cruise-ship design, sustainability, technologies, onboard dining or operations. But I won’t, because the people I admire most in cruising aren’t CEOs, managers or visionaries. They’re the butlers and housekeepers. The waiters and bartenders. The people you see swabbing the decks and dusting the potted plants. And the people you never see, who do the laundry, oil the engines and keep the sewage system running. I can’t speak too highly of cruise-ship crews. They’re the real journey makers. A ship can have designer furniture and lobster dinners but is nothing without good staff. The tireless work and smiles of the crew make the magic happen. Cruise-ship crews are the real journey makers. You could say that of any travel business, but cruise staff have added challenges. Housekeepers and waiters interact far more with customers than they ever would on land – and over many more days.



If a staff member feels seasick, too bad. If a huge swell makes food preparation in cramped galleys difficult, guests still expect dinner. Waiters cover 25 seats a shift, while explaining unfamiliar food and taking orders in a foreign language. 



Spare a thought for the crew working hard so you don’t have to. Passengers complain anyway, of course. And yes, customers are entitled to get what they pay for, and to make legitimate complaints. But first, spare a thought for the person who has confused your dessert order, or forgotten to empty the rubbish bin in your cabin. Related Article Cruises Twelve of the most incredible experiences you can do from a cruise ship Have patience. Be kind. Would it kill you to leave your cabin reasonably tidy to make the housekeeper’s life easier? To carry a towel from pool to laundry basket? And believe it or not, you won’t damage your wrist by lifting a plate, or overload your brain by remembering the butler’s name. Be friendly, but not excessively so. A long corridor conversation means the housekeeper has to work later to finish. Crew off the ship don’t want more than a hello: they only have a couple of hours with their friends, and you aren’t one of them. Leave a tip. Fill in your customer review, because crew rely on commendations to get promotions or their next contract. Your travel life is blessed by the hard work of others.

World.title: Technology is making cruising easier, but there’s an unspoken cost
World.content:
Travel newsCruises Technology is making cruising easier, but there’s an unspoken cost Brian Johnston September 15, 2026 — 9:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just about every cruise line now encourages guests to download an app on the promise, or premise, that it will ease organisation and onboard bookings, and tailor experiences as passengers see fit. It’s just one of the technologies taking over cruise ships, especially the bigger budget ships that have notably younger passengers. Luxury ships are heading that way too, although more sedately. As we get accustomed to increasing technology in our daily lives, we’re accepting more of this onboard revolution – after all, we ask Siri or Alexa questions, order Uber Eats, check-in via consoles, book online and point phones at menu QR codes. As we get increasingly used to integrating technology into our daily lives, we’re becoming more accepting of the onboard tech revolution. Similar interfaces are appearing all over cruise ships, from check-in, in public areas, via smart televisions in cabins, and on bracelets or other gadgets provided by cruise lines.



Biometrics greet us at the cruise terminal, with companies such as Celebrity, MSC and Royal Caribbean using facial recognition for check-in. Speed is the promised benefit, with Royal Caribbean touting “car to bar” in 10 minutes. 



In the cabins of some MSC ships you can tell the delightful voice-activated Zoe to turn on the lights, or ask her for information and advice, in seven languages. Related Article Opinion

Tripologist Is AI better at travel advice than me? I put it to the test Michael Gebicki The Tripologist All of this technology is supplied on the promise from cruise lines that it streamlines our onboard organisation, frees us from standing in queues at reception and delivers a more personalised experience. But is the technology helping us, or are we helping the technology? Is the result more freedom, or are we allowing our lives, once again, to become ever more spied upon and controlled by big business? You can see the advantage for the cruise lines. Operations are streamlined. Passengers book shore excursions and speciality restaurants, a job once done by crew. Passengers’ habits and preferences are tracked, which helps to drive revenue.



An MSC Cruises report about what cruising might look like in 2030 says ultra-personalisation via technologies will be omnipresent. Cabins will even be able to sense the mood of passengers by detecting their heart and pulse rates and facial expressions. Is that a boon or a dystopia? Customers will decide. But if I can no longer interact with crew members, I think I’ll feel a pleasant aspect of cruising has gone missing.

World.title: Cruises to the Med used to go to the same tired stops. That’s changing
World.content:
First up, let me say you could hardly get tired of cruising the Mediterranean. You could sail into Athens or Barcelona or anywhere in between a dozen times, and always find something different to see and do.

What is true however is that most cruise lines offer similar itineraries that take you to all the same ports in one half of the Mediterranean or the other – or regional parts of it, such as the Greek Islands, or French and Italian Rivieras.

Is that changing? I think so. While big ships continue on the same merry-go-round, smaller companies have started eyeing up alternative destinations that go beyond the standard circuits and get you away from the worst crowds.

Didima Bay on the Greek island of Chios.

World.title: ‘Certificate 3 in prostitution’: Teacher demoted and moved schools over comments
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland courts ‘Certificate 3 in prostitution’: Teacher demoted and moved schools over comments Julius Dennis September 15, 2026 — 10:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The head of a department at a Queensland school has lost his appeal of a decision to demote him and force him to change schools over a series of creepy comments he was found by the industrial relations commission to have made to female students, including that one could have a “Certificate 3 in prostitution”. Scott Alan Barnard also discussed his own nipple piercings, greek statues with erect penises, and told a student he was “glad it’s your butt warmth that I’m sitting in”. The comments were made at various times in 2023 and 2024 to year 11 and 12 students at an undisclosed state school, who said he told he had drawn other students naked, and found it strange there were less pregnant students now than when he was in school. A teacher has lost his appeal of a decision to demote him over inappropriate remarks. Phil Carrick According to the ruling, which he appealed to the Queensland Industrial Relations Commission (QIRC) earlier this year, he made further comments of a sexual nature to a Year 11 student in 2023.



The names of the students and the school Barnard taught at have been suppressed. “When ... student O sought your assistance with positioning paper for printing, you stated words to the effect that you thought as a girl she would ‘know plenty of positions’. Student O interpreted this to mean ‘sex positions’ and it caused her to feel uncomfortable and embarrassed,” it said. He also told another student she had nice lips, and asked students to locate some “faggots”, which he said meant sticks, not the derogatory slur for LGBTQIA+ persons. Barnard, who had been working for the education department since 2005, denied the conversations about the greek statues, making nude artworks, and the “positions” and prostitution comments. According to the ruling, Barnard had received a sexual harassment complaint in March 2024, and an internal investigation found he should be disciplined for the allegation he had engaged in inappropriate and unprofessional manner towards students, which he denied.



Barnard had not been formally disciplined before, but had been subject to management action in 2023 after he made inappropriate remarks about a student’s physique, and said, “why go to the strip club when you can go to the beach and women are practically naked anyway”, the previous year. In his appeal, Barnard argued he could not travel 50 minutes to his new school as he was the carer of a child with a disability, and he would have to teach outside his expertise. Commissioner Peter O’Neill refused the appeal, telling Barnard he should have raised the issue of his caring for the child during the show cause process, and he had waited too long to launch his appeal. The disciplinary decision was made in December, and took effect in March 2026, after which Barnard had 21 days to appeal the decision, but did not do so until April.
