World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant ‘M’ evidence to resume after court hears former 2GB broadcaster bought flowers weekly for former athlete
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Alan Jones’ criminal trial in the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney.

Jones, 85, is standing trial on 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching without consent relating to six male complainants over a 17-year period from 2003 to 2020. He denies the alleged physical acts occurred.

Jones, pictured on Monday, is standing trial on 22 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching. Steven Siewert

Yesterday, the third of the six complainants, a former athlete dubbed “M”, started giving evidence.

“M” returns to the witness box today. Yesterday, he told the court:

Jones kissed him on the corner of his mouth at an event in Sydney about a decade ago. “I think I froze at that time,” “M” said.

The court heard Jones texted him that night: “Great to see you. Sorry I didn’t catch up after, had to go back to work. You looked great. I love you, I hope you can feel my kisses darling xxxx.”

“M” replied: “Nice to see you too. I had a very long day today and I am pleased to be in bed now; thanks mate xoxo.” The conversation ended in “M” saying “let me know when we can catch up. Lots of love” and Jones replying: “I will darling. Big kisses forever.”

The court heard that Jones texted “M” on another occasion, after receiving a photo: “I love the photo. I love you. I want to kiss you for hours. That is beautiful. We must catch up darling [name] xxx”. “M” said he did not respond immediately. Hours later, Jones wrote: “I hope my message did not upset you. I love you.” The man said he responded the next day, writing: “Not at all mate. It’s nice to be loved.”

The complainant said he had used the word “mate” for many reasons. “I know I’d made it very clear that ... it wasn’t moving into a relationship, so ‘mate’ was my way of pushing back, I guess.”

“M” said that on the last occasion he visited Jones at his harbourside apartment, the broadcaster kissed him repeatedly on the cheek towards his lips and said words to the effect of, “I love you so much, you don’t know how much I love you.” The complainant said he could feel Jones’ genitals on his leg .

The complainant said he pushed the broadcaster away and said, “OK, mate”, in a tone intended to convey “get away from me”, and “got out of there as quickly as possible”.

The court heard Jones had sent the complainant gifts including weekly flowers for years and a dinner set. The complainant agreed he also sent Jones flowers at least once.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Frank, fearless, but not so free-style? Staff survey changes raise eyebrows
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic service Frank, fearless, but not so free-style? Staff survey changes raise eyebrows Matt Dennien Updated September 15, 2026 — 10:05am ,first published September 14, 2026 — 7:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to Brisbane Times’ Queensland public sector column, Public Circus. This week: a Working for Queensland survey prompt, “vacancy management” hits Child Safety, and wage ruling saga lands senior teachers on par with their juniors. It’s everyone’s favourite time of the year. No, not the seasonal change of spring – Working for Queensland survey month! By everyone, of course, we mean those with thoughts about their public sector employment they would maybe only dare lay out in the free-text general feedback box of the anonymised questionnaire. This year, however, it seems there could be a catch. Queensland public service HQ at One William Street. Matt Dennien Word has reached the Circus tent from multiple agencies the no-holds-barred rant box has disappeared from some surveys, or been replaced with a more restrictive prompt for others.



Since landing in inboxes from late August, some eager (only about 20 per cent of the 330,0000-strong workforce filled it out in 2025) and eagle-eyed public servants have clocked the curious changes. But it’s not uniform across the sector, with the separately collected free-text section included at the discretion of each agency and sent directly, unedited, to the boss. We’ve caught whispers some folks receiving surveys have this year found no open feedback section at the end. Other departments we’ve had intel from are said to have replaced the general feedback prompt with one asking what you’d tell someone considering a job there, or what is one thing you would change.



“It’s not as open-ended as it has been in previous years,” a department source said, speaking to us on condition of anonymity for perhaps the obvious reason of not being authorised to do so. Related Article Public service Returning kindness: The volunteers who emotionally rejuvenate Roma Street’s police They noted it seemed to be an attempt to steer staff away from airing more detailed or specific gripes. One former agency chief, also granted anonymity, told us they viewed it as one of the most important parts of the surveys because of the freeing, anonymised nature of the comments. They suggested any removal of or constraining of this would reflect a lack of willingness to “really hear what people think”.



With a couple of weeks left to complete, we imagine more will discover the changes as they open them closer to the due date – a practice Circus members are certainly not immune from on our workplace feedback forms, either. But what to do if you discover you’re cut off from the trauma dump you were hoping to give, or have already been confronted by such an injustice? We’ve got you covered. Fill out the form below (on a non-work device and network) and tell us instead. Drop contact details if you’re willing to talk more, anonymously, of course. We’ll even try and publish what we can in a future segment. Let the frank and fearless feedback flow!



‘Vacancy management’ comes for Child Safety frontline support roles Fresh on the heels of the state’s first credit rating downgrade in almost 20-years, Circus can add a seventh department to its list of those with various efforts in place to squeeze staffing budgets. The latest “vacancy management strategy” word (don’t call it a hiring freeze!) is from over at Belinda Drew’s Department of Families, Seniors, Disability Services and Child Safety. There, the strategy is said to review vacant roles across child safety, disability services and corporate support before they can be filled. Those not deemed “key frontline” require stricter approval. This includes sign-off by a deputy director-general and a documented rationale. So far, so similar to what we’ve heard from widely across the sector.



But the thing that has some child safety staff, and their union (Together), up in arms? What, exactly, is being classified as a frontline role under the exemption list. In particular, the lack of an exemption for administration and business officers in child safety service centres – who keep such centres, which support frontline child protection workers, running. “These roles are critical to frontline child protections, and they should be treated as critical workers when it comes time to fill them,” Together assistant secretary Dee Spink said in a statement. “The department says this isn’t a recruitment freeze, but for some workers it can feel like one.”



A department spokesperson said vacancy management was just one part of efforts to balance the books and ensure focus on its priorities, with all efforts to fill vacancies reviewed against workforce needs. For what it’s worth, we quizzed independent economist Saul Eslake about this vacancy management approach to belt-tightening while chatting to him on Friday about that credit downgrade. His view? “They’re a lazy way of trying to save money,” Eslake offered. “They’re fairly crude measures and not ones that I would ever support.” Eslake also reckoned the roughly 3 per cent staff expense growth projected from next financial year in Treasurer David Janetzki’s June budget (this year’s is 5.4 per cent) is only possible with a proper freeze on the size of the public service. Either that, or that slim surplus pencilled in for after the 2028 election might end up being kicked down the road – something we’re sure the ratings agencies will be watching closely.





The first band of this classification is available to those with two or more years of satisfactory service as a “senior teacher”. The second, EST 2, can be reached after three years at EST 1. That higher band was created in the 2019 agreement and is not reflected in the award. While EST 1 wages were set to lift through a safety net tied to the state wage case ruling, EST 2 wages were not. Then acting general secretary Brendan Crotty said the union clocked the issue weeks ago, raising it with Sharon Schimming’s apparently unaware department and Minister John-Paul Langbroek. Eventually, a departmental directive was issued to allow EST 2 teachers to get the higher award rate. This temporary fix, however, essentially leaves more senior teachers on an equal pay rate to those on a lower band until the difference can be sorted via the broader ongoing arbitration process. Yikes.



The issue has, as you might imagine, gone down like a tonne of lead pencils for teachers – some of whom have taken to the union’s social media comment sections to give an unfavourable report card of even some of the union process. Queensland teachers gather in Queen’s Park during the second of two Queensland Teachers’ Union strike days last year. Polina Levina/Getty Images “The QTU acknowledges that some members at EST 2 level may understandably feel frustrated that, for the time being, this means being paid at the same, if higher, rate as EST 1,” Crotty wrote to members last week. That “time being” is likely to still be some time yet, given arbitration hearings before the Queensland Industrial Relations Commission have now been given a start date of… April 6 next year. Have a curiosity for the Circus tent? Email on m.dennien@nine.com.au. For more security, sing out with a non-work device and network via Signal (mattdennien.15 or here) and mattdennien@protonmail.com. World.title: Why you should think twice before complaining on your next cruise
World.content:
Reviews & adviceCruises Why you should think twice before complaining on your next cruise Brian Johnston September 15, 2026 — 9:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I could name a dozen people who’ve had a significant influence on cruise-ship design, sustainability, technologies, onboard dining or operations. But I won’t, because the people I admire most in cruising aren’t CEOs, managers or visionaries. They’re the butlers and housekeepers. The waiters and bartenders. The people you see swabbing the decks and dusting the potted plants. And the people you never see, who do the laundry, oil the engines and keep the sewage system running. I can’t speak too highly of cruise-ship crews. They’re the real journey makers. A ship can have designer furniture and lobster dinners but is nothing without good staff. The tireless work and smiles of the crew make the magic happen. Cruise-ship crews are the real journey makers. You could say that of any travel business, but cruise staff have added challenges. Housekeepers and waiters interact far more with customers than they ever would on land – and over many more days.



If a staff member feels seasick, too bad. If a huge swell makes food preparation in cramped galleys difficult, guests still expect dinner. Waiters cover 25 seats a shift, while explaining unfamiliar food and taking orders in a foreign language. 



Spare a thought for the crew working hard so you don’t have to. Passengers complain anyway, of course. And yes, customers are entitled to get what they pay for, and to make legitimate complaints. But first, spare a thought for the person who has confused your dessert order, or forgotten to empty the rubbish bin in your cabin. Related Article Cruises Twelve of the most incredible experiences you can do from a cruise ship Have patience. Be kind. Would it kill you to leave your cabin reasonably tidy to make the housekeeper’s life easier? To carry a towel from pool to laundry basket? And believe it or not, you won’t damage your wrist by lifting a plate, or overload your brain by remembering the butler’s name. Be friendly, but not excessively so. A long corridor conversation means the housekeeper has to work later to finish. Crew off the ship don’t want more than a hello: they only have a couple of hours with their friends, and you aren’t one of them. Leave a tip. Fill in your customer review, because crew rely on commendations to get promotions or their next contract. Your travel life is blessed by the hard work of others.

World.title: Technology is making cruising easier, but there’s an unspoken cost
World.content:
Travel newsCruises Technology is making cruising easier, but there’s an unspoken cost Brian Johnston September 15, 2026 — 9:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Just about every cruise line now encourages guests to download an app on the promise, or premise, that it will ease organisation and onboard bookings, and tailor experiences as passengers see fit. It’s just one of the technologies taking over cruise ships, especially the bigger budget ships that have notably younger passengers. Luxury ships are heading that way too, although more sedately. As we get accustomed to increasing technology in our daily lives, we’re accepting more of this onboard revolution – after all, we ask Siri or Alexa questions, order Uber Eats, check-in via consoles, book online and point phones at menu QR codes. As we get increasingly used to integrating technology into our daily lives, we’re becoming more accepting of the onboard tech revolution. Similar interfaces are appearing all over cruise ships, from check-in, in public areas, via smart televisions in cabins, and on bracelets or other gadgets provided by cruise lines.



Biometrics greet us at the cruise terminal, with companies such as Celebrity, MSC and Royal Caribbean using facial recognition for check-in. Speed is the promised benefit, with Royal Caribbean touting “car to bar” in 10 minutes. 



In the cabins of some MSC ships you can tell the delightful voice-activated Zoe to turn on the lights, or ask her for information and advice, in seven languages. Related Article Opinion

Tripologist Is AI better at travel advice than me? I put it to the test Michael Gebicki The Tripologist All of this technology is supplied on the promise from cruise lines that it streamlines our onboard organisation, frees us from standing in queues at reception and delivers a more personalised experience. But is the technology helping us, or are we helping the technology? Is the result more freedom, or are we allowing our lives, once again, to become ever more spied upon and controlled by big business? You can see the advantage for the cruise lines. Operations are streamlined. Passengers book shore excursions and speciality restaurants, a job once done by crew. Passengers’ habits and preferences are tracked, which helps to drive revenue.



An MSC Cruises report about what cruising might look like in 2030 says ultra-personalisation via technologies will be omnipresent. Cabins will even be able to sense the mood of passengers by detecting their heart and pulse rates and facial expressions. Is that a boon or a dystopia? Customers will decide. But if I can no longer interact with crew members, I think I’ll feel a pleasant aspect of cruising has gone missing.

World.title: 'Absolutely appalled' - Labour's Chris Hipkins unleashes on Oranga Tamariki's 'systemic issues'
World.content:
Labour's Chris Hipkins is calling on Oranga Tamariki's boss to fix the "systemic issues" in the agency after RNZ revealed staff were present during the assault of a young person by his peers in a ritual attack known as 'walking the line'.

The young person had been slapped and hit by other teenagers as he was discharged from youth justice residence Korowai Manaaki in March, RNZ revealed last month.

The ministry told RNZ the "action or inaction" in this case was being addressed and it could not provide further details about why staff did not stop the assault.

Hipkins told RNZ on Tuesday morning he had been "absolutely appalled" at what he had heard about the incident.

"Oranga Tamariki have had decades of reports indicating that they need to do better. They're still not fixing that.

"We have to drive a much greater focus on improving the way things are operating in youth residential facilities," he told RNZ.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told RNZ the ministry had been going through real challenges for at least a decade and "there's been a number of reviews".

"We've got an excellent new CEO there...and is making sure that any reviews are followed up and actually actions are implemented."

But Hipkins said not enough had been done to "improve the way things are operating in youth residential facilities".

Asked why Labour in government didn't shut the youth residences down when that has been the advice in previous reviews, Hipkins said "because you've still got to have somewhere for these very vulnerable kids to go".

While he wouldn't comment on individual staff at the facilities Hipkins said, "clearly there are some systemic issues here that are deep-seated, have been around a long time, and still need to be addressed".

He said it was for the agency's chief executive to fix the "systemic issue".

While it was months ago when the assault at Korowai Manaaki took took place, no staff present when it happened reported it to the resident manager.

That only happened in July, when a youth raised it was a team leader.

A young person was slapped and hit by other teenagers as he was discharged from Korowai Manaaki in March. RNZ/Peter de Graaf

In official Oranga Tamariki (OT) documents seen by RNZ the 'walking the line' assault is explained as a situation where young people stand either side of the internal door of the main entrance to the unit and wait to farewell the young person being discharged.

In this instance, three young people stood on one side and two on the other. The document described the young person being discharged as standing at the top of the line. It said "he appeared nervous and was hesitant to walk towards the door".

The incident was referred to police and an employment investigation had commenced.

RNZ requested further information about the assault, and was told that at the time of the incident in question, "kaimahi were present in the unit with the rangatahi".

OT also confirmed police had closed their investigation with no charges made and no further action, advising OT they found "no evidence of criminal offending by either the rangatahi involved or the kaimahi".

At the time of the request made to OT for further information in mid-August, OT said an employment process was still underway regarding the matter.

RNZ then asked why staff did not stop the assault from happening.

Oranga Tamariki Youth Justice Services and Residential Care deputy chief executive Dean Winter responded, saying "staff action or inaction in this case is being addressed appropriately and we cannot provide further details".

World.title: Possible hung parliament as Labour and National slump in latest poll
World.content:
Both major parties are below the 30 percent mark with less than two months until the election, according to a new poll.

The latest The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll, funded by Infrastructure New Zealand, shows neither the current coalition bloc nor the opposition bloc would have the numbers to form a government, with both blocs on 60 seats.

Since the last of this poll in June, Labour has slumped by 7 points. It remains in the lead, but only just.

National has also fallen, by 2 points, while the Greens, New Zealand First, and ACT have all gone up.

For the first time in this poll, the Opportunity Party is above the 5 percent threshold, but its numbers are still not enough to help the left bloc into government.

Labour: 28 percent (down 7)

National: 27 percent (down 2)

Greens: 14 percent (up 4)

NZ First: 13 percent (up 1)

ACT: 9 percent (up 1)

Opportunity: 6 percent (previously included with 'other')

Te Pāti Māori: 2 percent (no change)

Other: 2 percent (down 1)

According to The Post's calculations, which assume that parties win electorate seats broadly in line with their share of the party vote, and retain at least one electorate seat each, the coalition bloc would have 60 seats, while the parliamentary opposition would have 53. Add in Opportunity's 7 and that leads to a hung Parliament.

Those numbers could change if there is an overhang, as Te Pāti Māori has been campaigning on.

In the preferred prime minister stakes, Chris Hipkins is on 45 percent, up 1 point from June's poll. Christopher Luxon is down 2 points to 35 percent. A further 16 percent of people chose neither, while 4 percent were unsure.

A majority of voters also still believe the country is heading in the wrong direction, with 56 percent saying so. Those feeling the country is heading in the right direction numbered 27 percent.

National Party campaign manager Simeon Brown is dismissing the poll, saying the the only poll that matters is election day, and National remains focused on winning.

Freshwater Strategy interviewed n=1011 eligible voters in New Zealand, aged 18+ online, between 4-11 September. The margin of error was +/- 3 percent. The data is weighted to be representative of New Zealand voters.

Luxon was reluctant to discuss the poll with reporters at Parliament on Tuesday, saying he remained focused on "the only poll that matters" - the election.

"I don't comment on polls," he said.

"You may think that's important to you. It's not important to me."

Luxon insisted he was getting a "great reaction" from New Zealanders on the ground and felt "really positive" about the road ahead.

"I'm enjoying this campaign, loving getting out and about and seeing people and finding out how actually how we help them."

Hipkins was more reflective, acknowledging Labour needed to lift its performance in the poll.

"It's not where we need it to be. We're going to be fighting hard to get our numbers up," he said. "Look, I'm happy that we're ahead of National, but I want us to do significantly better than that."

Hipkins said Labour would be fighting hard to earn every vote. He believed New Zealanders were upset with the "whole political establishment" right now.

"They are working hard, they are playing by the rules, they're doing everything right, and they feel like they're going backwards.

World.title: Tauranga Hospital Emergency Department staff declare 'state of emergency'
World.content:
Emergency Department staff at Tauranga Hospital have declared "a state of emergency", warning of the risks of an ED which they say is often running at 150-200 percent of its capacity, without the staffing needed.

More than 100 Nurses Organisation (NZNO) members and ED staff at the hospital have written a letter to Health New Zealand's (HNZ) CEO Dale Bramley last Tuesday about their concerns.

The letter said the ED hasn't received the extra nursing staff required, as identified in "Care Capacity Demand Management" (CCDM) assessments over the past two years.

It said a patient collapsing in the ED wait room toilet was a stark reminder of the risks when overcrowding becomes normalised, and the ED is required to operate beyond their capacity everyday.

NZNO delegate John Wylie said staff being asked to assess and treat some patients in corridors have become routine practice due to the ongoing patient flow pressures.

"We are often working at more than 150-200% capacity, and I cannot recall any recent day when the ED was not running at over 100% capacity," he said.

The letter urged HNZ to approve the hiring of more nurses, based on calculations from the previous CCDMs.

The 2025/2026 modelling found that 13.66 more roles were needed - across nurses and health care assistants, and the 2026/2027 modelling found 16.78 more roles were needed.

The NZNO is advocating for a change in Government.

A response from Dale Bramley, dated a day after he received the letter from the workers, said he'd recently visited the Tauranga Hospital ED.

He said he'd had conversations with staff about the challenges on the frontline.

"I acknowledge the sustained pressures experienced by the department and the impact these can have on both staff wellbeing and the delivery of patient care,

"Ensuring Tauranga ED has the workforce and resources it needs to provide safe, high-quality care is a priority," he said in the letter.

Bramley said decisions on staffing sit with the regional director for Midland - Cath Cronin - and the interim group director of operations for Bay of Plenty, Jo Gibbs.

He said he'd asked Cronin and Gibbs to meet with staff, and agree on the way forward on uplifting staff numbers.

"I have asked that this meeting occurs within a fortnight," said Bramley in the letter.

World.title: Nicola Willis hints National to campaign on income bracket changes, research tax credit
World.content:
Nicola Willis has hinted National will campaign on changes to the research and development tax credit after businesses hailed its success.

She also indicated changes to income tax brackets.

Business NZ's election conference in Wellington began with a political panel on the economy, with National's Willis, Labour's Barbara Edmonds, ACT's David Seymour, New Zealand First's Shane Jones, the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick and Opportunity's Qiulae Wong.

Te Pāti Māori was not represented.

The politicians were asked what one tax or regulatory change they would make that would support businesses.

"I've got a newsworthy thing to say," said Willis, pointing to Business NZ's election manifesto which she said reflected the success of the research and development tax credit.

The tax credit incentivises science and technology research and development.

Willis said businesses clearly valued it, and it was supporting innovation.

"We will wait until after the pre-election fiscal update (on 29 September) to make a specific announcement, but that's the next cab off the rank for me," she said.

Willis also said National would address "bracket creep" which is when inflation pushes people into higher tax brackets.

Adjusting tax settings would ensure "working people on average wages aren't being slapped with bigger and larger effective taxes every year," she said.

"After the pre-election update, I will have more to say."

Seymour supported using extra revenue from bracket creep to flatten tax rates so more people paid similar amounts, while Jones warned against reducing revenue without reducing costs "given the challenges that we've already got".

On tax policy, Edmonds referred to Labour's already-announced capital gains tax, which would also "streamline" land rules in the Income Tax Act and give businesses certainty.

Seymour pointed to ACT pushing the government to cut red tape, including reforms in holiday and health and safety laws, the Resource Management Act, and fast-track legislation.

Jones said he was proud that "no more voice was louder than mine in ridding these unwanted burdensome ideological climate change reporting standards that had been imposed on New Zealand firms".

Swarbrick said the Greens would boost market competition particularly in the energy and supermarket sectors.

World.title: Oranga Tamariki staff present during 'walking the line' assault
World.content:
Oranga Tamariki has confirmed staff were present during the assault of a young person by his peers in a ritual attack known as 'walking the line'.

The ministry told RNZ the "action or inaction" in this case was being addressed and it could not provide further details about why staff did not stop the assault.

RNZ revealed last month that a young person had been slapped and hit by other teenagers as he was discharged from youth justice residence Korowai Manaaki in March.

Official Oranga Tamariki (OT) documents seen by RNZ confirmed that a 'walking the line' assault took place.

That was explained as a situation where young people stand either side of the internal door of the main entrance to the unit and wait to farewell the young person being discharged.

In this instance, three young people stood on one side and two on the other.

The document described the young person being discharged as standing at the top of the line. It said "he appeared nervous and was hesitant to walk towards the door".

The incident was referred to police and an employment investigation had commenced.

RNZ requested further information about the assault, and was told that at the time of the incident in question, "kaimahi were present in the unit with the rangatahi".

OT also confirmed police had closed their investigation with no charges made and no further action, advising OT they found "no evidence of criminal offending by either the rangatahi involved or the kaimahi".

At the time of the request made to OT for further information in mid-August, OT said an employment process was still underway regarding the matter.

RNZ then asked why staff did not stop the assault from happening.

Oranga Tamariki Youth Justice Services and Residential Care deputy chief executive Dean Winter responded, saying "staff action or inaction in this case is being addressed appropriately and we cannot provide further details".

World.title: ASB chief executive Vittoria Shortt stepping down
World.content:
ASB chief executive Vittoria Shortt is stepping down after almost nine years in the role, with Commonwealth Bank executive Sinead Taylor appointed as her replacement.

Shortt will finish on 11 December, with Taylor taking over as chief executive and managing director the following day.

Taylor has held a number of senior positions within ASB's parent company, Commonwealth Bank of Australia.

She is currently group executive of its institutional banking and markets division, and has previously held roles across strategy, marketing, business and corporate banking.

Taylor was born in Glasgow, Scotland, and lived for a number of years in New Zealand after moving to Rotorua at the age of nine.

ASB chair Dame Therese Walsh paid tribute to Shortt, acknowledging her work and dedication as chief executive and as a former ASB board member.

Walsh said Taylor was well qualified to take over the role, having led large teams and complex transformation projects.

"That combination of customer focus, operational discipline and execution makes her well placed to lead ASB through its next phase," she said.

Vittoria Shortt plans to take a break after stepping down before deciding on her next career move.

"I'm looking forward to some travel, starting with a roadie around New Zealand, and spending more time with my family. I want to take some time to consider my next move professionally."

World.title: Explainer: Why is everyone talking about AI and the end of the world?
World.content:
Explainer - The debate over artificial intelligence and how dangerous it is has reached warp speed in the past few days.

The head of one of the world's biggest AI companies is calling for development to slow down as some warn the technology "could kill us all", while US President Donald Trump has dismissed anti-AI rhetoric as "sick".

Many say the debate is getting increasingly urgent.

"I think it's the most important thing happening in the world right now," John Steidley, an AI researcher at Californian nonprofit Palisade Research, told RNZ's Morning Report.

It's all moving incredibly fast, but here's a quick look at what has triggered the latest rounds of AI concern and what power brokers and politicians are saying.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for AI development to slow down. MICHAEL M. SANTIAGO/AFP

Why is everyone suddenly freaking out?

Dario Amodei, the CEO of leading AI company Anthropic, posted an essay over the weekend urging developers to slow down and add safety standards.

It's set off a firestorm of debate from the White House on down on a technology that is making headline news around the world, but is moving so fast that it's difficult for many people to even fully understand what it's doing.

"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Amodei wrote, putting forward a three-step plan that would call for independent evaluators over safety, coordination between firms over their own standards and international cooperation to manage AI risks.

Understanding risk of self-replicating artificial intelligence Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said they agreed with Amodei's concerns.

"The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade," said Jacob Coxon, who had worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic before he posted his warning on social media.

That warning has echoed around the world in the past week.

"In AI, governments, companies and the rich (mainly) men behind them are chasing geopolitical, military and financial advantage by building it as fast as possible," the ABC's Alan Kohler wrote in an analysis piece published by RNZ.

A backlash has been growing against AI's expansion, its effect on the environment and employment, as well as the lack of safeguards over the industry.

US President Donald Trump, on the other hand, has taken a far more laissez-faire approach to AI regulation, claiming there is a "sick conspiracy" against the technology. He's said America must "win" the AI war against China and dismissed concerns about data centres.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Matt Ramey / AFP

What are some of the fears about AI?

The two biggest fears about AI are around deliberate malicious deployment by humans or, more worryingly, autonomous replication by AI agents acting on their own initiative, Steidley said.

A hacking incident in July by what was called "rogue" AI made news around the world.

OpenAI said that one of its experimental models broke out of a testing space and hacked into an AI startup called Hugging Face.

Connor Leahy, an AI expert and the US director of Control AI, told the ABC that the attack was "crazy".

"The idea that something could just, without human oversight, escape from something like this and then autonomously decide to attack a different company is kind of unheard of."

Steidley said that attack was a red flag for many in the AI field.

"I think one thing that we're very fortunate to have is this example of the Hugging Face attack from July, where AI got out of control and that gives us a chance to respond to that without any humans being severely harmed."

There have been concerns about it being used to create new kinds of biological weapons or access nuclear weapons.

There's also fears about the enormous amount of money being poured into AI and that it's creating a bubble in the stock market that will eventually burst, causing global financial chaos.

"I have a lot of hope that we can solve these problems, but we have to make sure that we don't move so fast that no human can keep up with what's happening," Steidley said.

Is the panic overblown?

That very much depends on who you ask.

Timrit Gebru, an AI researcher and former Google employee, recently told Wired magazine that the talk of humanity's extinction at the hands of "machine-gods" is meant as a distraction from real issues it contributes to like climate change and job losses.

"Bosses are using AI as an excuse to get rid of their pesky workers," she told Wired.

Internet big-picture writer and essayist Cory Doctorow has criticised the "AI-pocalypse" narratives and claims that AI is somehow "alive," calling LLMs (large language models) "a very sophisticated word-guessing programme" and accusing companies of fear-mongering to raise their profile and stock value.

"Remember: every time you repeat a story about how awfully, terribly dangerous their products are, you help them raise more investment capital, which is a key input for their business (hooking up statistical engines to money-furnaces)," he wrote in a recent newsletter.

However, Steidley said that the world still needs to come up with regulatory framework for AI, and fast.

"I think we're not quite at the point where we cannot stop AIs from doing things we don't want, because they're not quite more capable than we are, which is to say that we still have time. We still have time to avert these disasters before AI is so smart that it can outsmart us.

"I think what the world needs is international coordination so no country or AI company in any country builds AI that it can't control that's smarter than humans.

"That's what we did with the nuclear situation. We didn't just let any country have nukes."

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said he is "concerned" about the dangers of AI, but also sees opportunities. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

What's New Zealand's position on all this, then?

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has been a steady advocate for adopting AI within New Zealand.

Asked at Monday's press conference if he was worried about AI wiping out humanity, Luxon said "No, no I'm not."

Luxon said he felt AI offered enormous potential for New Zealand to boost its productivity, but admitted to some concerns.

"Yes, we are concerned about the dangers of AI, but I would just say we see the opportunities as being greater than the dangers at this point in time."

Luxon said New Zealand "needs to work with like-minded friends to put in place the right regulatory frameworks."

He said discussions are ongoing with Five Eyes partners and cybersecurity experts.

"It's been good to actually hear, even in the last week, that those three big CEOs of the major AI firms are actually saying 'Hey listen, we want to slow this down so that companies and governments can actually keep up to speed.'"

Luxon said that businesses also need to be sure they're investing in their own cybersecurity as possible AI-related threats evolve.

The government unveiled a national AI strategy last year, which promised a "light-touch and principles-based" approach using existing legislation and regulations, rather than introducing new ones.

Dr Andrew Lensen, a senior lecturer in Artificial Intelligence at Victoria University, said then that the strategy was heavy on economic growth opportunities but "worryingly light" on ethical and societal issues.

"The strategy suggests that new legislation is unnecessary, which I, and many other AI researchers, disagree with," Lensen said.

For its part, Labour has promised if elected to government to set up an AI office, an online safety regulator, copyright rules that ensure creators are paid for their work, and impose rules on data centres.

"Used well, AI has huge benefits," leader Chris Hipkins said.

World.title: Llamas reduce number of dog attacks on sheep on Auckland council farms
World.content:
The Auckland council farms - or parks - have successfully reduced the number of roaming dog attacks on ewes and lambs thanks to six protective llamas that were introduced last year.

And another success story instituted by the council's farming business manager this year is a new special breed of lambs frolicking around paddocks - ones that produce less methane when they burp.

Mozz Trueman said there was 1500 hectares of farmland to manage and he had changed the breed of rams from Coopworths to Romney's which were hardier and had a quiet temperament.

Trueman said that the new rams also came from a special breeding programme called 'Cool Sheep' and were better for the environment.

The rams had been part of a trial for eight years and the data showed they literally had a lower carbon footprint, he said.

"That was the attraction for us. The easier thing to do would be to drop our stock rates but the income from that would affect our revenue.

"We started purchasing the low methane rams last year. So the lambs coming out this season are our first from the low methane programme," he said.

The llamas round the sheep up and protect them by getting between the threat and the sheep. Auckland Council

"We will start measuring them once we have finished docking and we have got the final tallies in - so we can get a number. I think as an entity we all need to get across it so we know how much we are emitting."

Trueman said unique security guards had been bought to protect the flocks of special lambs. He calls them Llama-guards.

This follows a horrific attack last June when three roaming dogs killed 142 lambs and injured another 86 in two attacks at Puhinui Reserve in Manukau.

At the time park rangers moved the surviving sheep to another site to keep them safe, and relocated others to a more visible part of the park. Trueman estimated the financial loss to be around $19,000.

"As you can appreciate we have a lot of roaming dogs. But since we have had llamas they have protected the sheep. We have a couple of incidents this year where we have lost seven lambs - as opposed to losing that 140 in one night."

He said llamas would push the sheep into a corner to keep them safe and then go towards the dogs.

"They do stand up tall and make a weird bugle sounding warning noise. They can get really aggressive."

A ewe lamb with her mum at Duder Regional Park. Auckland Council

Trueman said in the paddocks where the llamas grazed with the sheep - there had not been any dog attacks.

The council's land had up to 6 million people visiting each year - and everyone was welcome, he said. However he described it as "farming in a fish bowl" - which had its challenges.

He said people who were not familiar with how farming worked could sometimes think they were helping lambs and calves - but they were not.

World.title: India refuses to accept Asia Cup cricket trophy from Pakistani minister
World.content:
Political tensions between India and Pakistan have spilled onto the cricket field again, with India's women refusing to accept the Asia Cup trophy from Asian Cricket Council (ACC) chairman Mohsin Naqvi.

India dominated from the start to win the tournament for a record eighth time, beating Sri Lanka by 72 runs in the final in Dubai.

After winning the toss, India scored 5-183 before dismissing Sri Lanka for 111 in 20 overs.

The presentation ceremony was delayed nearly an hour, during which the Indian team conducted its own medal presentation, with Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia presenting the best fielder medal to Nandani Sharma.

Naqvi — chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board and the ACC, as well as Pakistan's interior minister — stood on the dais with several ACC officials, but the Indian team did not appear to receive medals or the trophy, with social media footage showing them leaving the field as the officials waited on stage.

The ceremony ended abruptly after medals were presented to the Sri Lankan team and match officials, and Naqvi presented the runners-up cheque to Sri Lanka captain Chamari Athapaththu.

"This is BCCI's stand [to not take trophy from Naqvi]. We can't say anything on this," India coach Amol Muzumdar said.

"India are officially the champions. Trophy or no trophy doesn't matter to us.

"For us, this tournament is over, we are the champions. That's good enough. It was on the big board that India are the champions of Asia Cup 2026."

Cross-border tensions between India and Pakistan brought the two countries to the brink of war last year, with the acrimony also spilling onto the cricket field. Indian cricketers have avoided handshakes with Pakistan players and refused to accept the trophy and medals from a Pakistani official at several tournaments.

The Indian men's team beat Pakistan three times in the Asia Cup, including the final, but Suryakumar Yadav's team refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi and did not shake hands with Pakistan players in any of the three games.

The Indian women's team did not shake hands with the Pakistan team in its match earlier in the tournament, after which Muzumdar also said: "That stand has been taken by BCCI and we stand by it."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: The Stinear effect: The stat changing Geelong in 2026
World.content:
The biggest coup of the off-season wasn't Anne Hatchard to Gold Coast, Taylor Smith to Sydney, or Eden Zanker to Fremantle.

It was premiership coach Mick Stinear's shift away from Melbourne to take the reins at Geelong.

He became the first coach to be poached by another club, leaving his position to take up another, and just the third coach to ply their trade at a second club.

The reasons behind Geelong's desperation to appoint Stinear have been immediately evident. Outside of a big round one loss to two-time reigning premier North Melbourne, the Cats have found their feet in a new style.

And although there have been early challenges on the injury front — the club has been forced to name top up players in its extended squad already this year — the system itself has proved sound.

Stinear's signature stat

Aishling Moloney has been a vital goal kicker for the Cats. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Josh Chadwick)

Teams coached by Stinear have one thing in common: Goal Assists are a priority. Sharing the ball neatly around the attacking arc to generate the highest percentage opportunity to score has always been fundamental to how his teams work, and that has already become a feature of Geelong in 2026.

Leading Melbourne for the first 10 seasons of its life in the AFLW, the Demons sat in the top two for goal assists in four of the five seasons from 2022 S6 onward. The one outlier was 2024, where the club was desperately stretched due to an onslaught of injury.

Melbourne's Goal Assists Avg. goal assists AFLW rank AFLW average 2025 5.3 2 3.6 2024 3.1 8 3.0 2023 6.3 1 3.4 2022 (S7) 4.2 1 2.6 2022 (S6) 3.9 2 2.5

This year the Cats average 7.8 goal assists — sitting second in the league behind only North Melbourne — and as a result, a host of other key scoring statistics have improved dramatically.

Aishling Moloney leads the way for the stat, with 1.6 per game, while having also kicked seven goals in the opening five games, but there are a total of seven Cats averaging 0.6 goal assists or more in that time.

Only two Geelong players averaged 0.6 or more goal assists across the 2025 AFLW season; Julia Crockett-Grills with 1.0, and Moloney with 0.6.

Julia Crockett-Grills averaged one goal assist per game in the 2025 AFLW season. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Elsby)

Because of this increased willingness to bring teammates in and create those deeper forward entries by way of looking for goal assist opportunities, Geelong is kicking more than four more goals per game in 2026, and goaling more regularly from the inside 50s it creates than in years gone past.

In five games the Cats have already kicked 50 goals. They kicked 69 across the whole of 2025.

They have made a marginal improvement on average inside 50s, but it is what they are doing once in the arc that has been the real difference.

Geelong's growing attack Avg. Points For Avg. Inside 50s Avg. Goal Efficiency (%) Avg. Goal Assists Avg. Goal Accuracy (%) Avg. Goal Kickers 2026 66.2 36.2 27.6 7.8 55.0 6.4 2025 41.7 32.6 17.7 3.4 36.3 4.1 2024 43.6 32.6 19.0 4.2 44.7 4.3 2023* 44.9 33.8 18.9 4.5 41.3 4.6

*Geelong reached the preliminary final

Getting it there

Obviously, to create these opportunities ahead of the ball, movement up the field needs to be more effective.

The Cats currently sit number one in the AFLW for disposal efficiency at an average of 69.8 per cent — this is something that the club has prided itself on in recent years.

The Cats move the ball via the hand a lot more under Mick Stinear. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/James Elsby)

The shift in disposal, however, has come via the method. A greater reliance on moving the ball by hand has been clear, with a league-low kick rate of 54.5 per cent, and a significant increase in uncontested possession indicates greater control outside the contest.

Issues of recent years are still present — ruck availability and strength is still a concern, clearance numbers have only marginally grown compared to 2025 — but the capacity to adapt on the outside has been the difference.

Outside ball Avg. uncontested possession Avg. contested possession rate (%) 2026 166.0 41.8 2025 136.4 45.8 2024 124.3 45.8 2023 131.5 46.0

Generating and scoring from turnover is a clear point of improvement, with the Cats averaging 24.0 points per game from the source in 2025 compared to its 42.6 points this year.

From turnover, they are effectively getting on the move, handballing to runners, and going quickly.

Becky Webster's work across the half back line, to intercept and drive the ball forward has been crucial in this respect, as has Mikayla Bowen's hard two-way running efforts while also carrying a heavy load through the midfield.

Not yet the complete package

Mick Stinear has moved to the Cats from Melbourne. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

While there are plenty of positive signs when it comes to Geelong's attacking game, there is still room for improvement in its defensive phase.

Conceding higher scores, more inside 50s, and more marks in the opposition's attacking zone, there is a vulnerability when sides can get the ball moving quickly against them.

There is an element of high risk, high reward in the game style the Cats have employed this year, and they are only five matches into the system, but protecting that defence more effectively is surely high on Stinear's priority list as they continue through the season.

Opposition attack Avg. Points Against Avg. Inside 50s Conceded Avg. Marks Inside 50s Conceded Avg. Shot Efficiency Conceded (%) 2026 53.8 38.4 9.6 50.0 2025 44.9 33.4 7.5 40.9 2024 39.7 30.7 6.3 44.4 2023 33.4 27.5 5.5 43.9

It is worth mentioning that after the Cats' round one loss to powerhouse North Melbourne, their average score conceded is in fact 42.3 points, indicating an improvement in that area.

But as the old adage goes; to be the best, you have to beat the best.

Come finals, this system needs to be able to stand up to what North Melbourne — or Stinear's old side Melbourne — has to offer.

There is every indication to suggest it can, but without a match against the Demons fixtured in the home and away season, and the Roos already in the rear view mirror, finals will be the chance to really test the system once more.

World.title: SA Health employee reprimanded for accessing Tony Modra's medical records
World.content:
One SA Health employee has been reprimanded for accessing AFL legend Tony Modra's private medical records after he was seriously injured in a truck crash, while two other employees remain under investigation, the health department says.

In a statement, SA Health said another six people were no longer being investigated.

"The number of employees under investigation for potentially accessing a patient's medical record inappropriately has been revised from nine individuals, to three," the statement said.

"Of these three, one individual has been reprimanded and two are still being investigated.

"Six individuals are no longer under investigation for this matter."

Any sanction imposed becomes part of an employee's permanent record.

Tony Modra spent time in hospital after the crash, and later shared a photo of himself in intensive care on Instagram. (Instagram: tonymodraofficial)

In July SA Health said nine staff were being either investigated for alleged inappropriate access to the records, or "assessed" to determine whether their access was "always appropriate".

At the time, the department also apologised to Modra's family for "any distress caused".

Modra underwent facial surgery and was in hospital for days after a truck crash at Back Valley, near Victor Harbor on South Australia's Fleurieu Peninsula, on June 18.

In July, the Crows legend posted an update of his progress on Instagram. In that post he said he was now able to get "out and about", and shared photos of himself in intensive care and recovering with his family.

In a statement earlier that month, he said he was "overwhelmed by the kindness and care" that he, and his family, had been shown.

Modra played a total of 165 AFL games for Adelaide and the Fremantle Dockers, after debuting for the Crows in 1992.

Police were called to the scene of the truck crash, near Victor Harbor, on June 18. (Supplied: SA Police)

The probe into staff accessing Modra's records is not the first time concerns have been raised about SA Health staff inappropriately accessing patient records in cases involving well-known people.

In 2016, 13 hospital staff were sanctioned after they were caught snooping on the medical records of Cy Walsh.

Cy Walsh had been charged with the stabbing murder of his father — Crows coach Phil Walsh — before being found not guilty by reason of mental incompetence.

In 2024, ABC News revealed a SA Health investigation had found 18 staff engaged in misconduct or inappropriately accessed the medical records of a patient understood to be Charlie Stevens, the late son of SA Police Commissioner Grant Stevens.

The department has also previously said it regularly conducted audits "to ensure that staff are accessing appropriate information".

World.title: Star Hawk's season over after ACL injury
World.content:
Three-time All-Australian Emily Bates will miss the rest of the AFLW season with a knee injury in a huge blow to Hawthorn's chances of snaring a maiden premiership.

Scans have confirmed Bates tore the anterior cruciate ligament in her right knee when the leg twisted awkwardly in a tackle during the Hawks' win over the Western Bulldogs on Saturday.

The 30-year-old club captain also damaged the meniscus and will undergo surgery.

"This is clearly disappointing news for Emily," Hawks AFLW general manager Keegan Brooksby said.

"The playing group and wider club will support her through the recovery journey.

"We have no doubt she'll approach her rehab with the diligence and professionalism she's always been known for.

Emily Bates played her 100th game for the Hawks against Adelaide. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

"Although Emily won't return to the field in 2026, she will continue to play an important off-field role in our program, as our captain."

Hawthorn face a huge test against AFLW juggernaut North Melbourne in Cairns on Friday night without Bates and Laura Stone (concussion).

Fellow midfielder Daisy Flockhart also has to prove her fitness after suffering a knock to her chest against the Bulldogs.

"We've been playing different players through [the midfield] and trying to build some versatility in our side … we're confident in the players we'll have in there," Hawks coach Daniel Webster said post-match on Saturday.

"It'll be a good challenge next week with who we're playing.

"We'll probably have some sort of different look in there with different players and that's OK. We'll keep getting to work."

Hawthorn (3-2) sit eighth in their quest for another finals berth, while North Melbourne (5-0) are in familiar territory on top of the ladder.

AAP

World.title: 'Bittersweet' Swans captaincy call for Rampe
World.content:
Dane Rampe didn't think Sydney would still be here, let alone that he'd be tasked with leading the Swans to an unlikely AFL premiership again.

A heart-and-soul player, veteran defender Rampe will stand in for an injured Callum Mills and captain the club in Friday's preliminary final against Fremantle at the SCG.

Rampe had led the Swans to the eventual 2024 grand final loss when a luckless Mills suffered a hamstring strain before that year's preliminary final.

But the circumstances surrounding this year's premiership push wildly differ.

Mills's vice-captain Isaac Heeney is among five Swans players serving club-imposed bans after last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Many in the AFL world had written off Sydney in the lead-up to finals, with even club chairman Andrew Pridham believing their chances had been "torpedoed".

Swans show what 'Bloods' culture is supposed to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

A gutsy 53-point qualifying final win over Brisbane went some way towards rebuilding respect for the club, especially after Mills suffered an ACL injury in the first quarter.

Sustained by the grit displayed against the back-to-back reigning premiers, Rampe was given the nod by Mills, coach Dean Cox and club leaders.

The former Swans co-captain is chasing his maiden premiership after playing in four grand final defeats (2014, 2016, 2022 and 2024).

"It's a thrill. It's a privilege. And yeah, it's a little bit bittersweet," Rampe said on Monday.

"The overwhelming emotion is probably just gratitude to be back here.

"Probably a month ago, we weren't sure what was going to happen with the team and with the club and with the players.

"To be here and challenging in a prelim is just something, particularly being at the back end of my career, I'm really grateful for."

Callum Mills may miss all of the 2027 season, or at least a sizable portion of it. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Rampe's return to captaincy comes after being re-drafted as a rookie by the Swans with fellow defender Jake Lloyd at the end of last year.

While Lloyd has signed on for a 15th season, neither Rampe nor the Swans have made a call on whether he will continue next year.

But the door is open, with defender Mills facing the possibility of missing the entire 2027 season.

"I haven't had a chance to think about that. I don't think it [being captain] does much," Rampe said.

"We'll wait and see. I'm just happy to be where I am at the moment and to have that little bit of hope and belief is, I feel, a real luxury."

Drafted at age 22 in 2013, Rampe was named co-captain with Josh Kennedy and Luke Parker for the 2019 season.

The trio handed the reins to Mills at the end of 2023, but their successor endured a tough 2024 season pockmarked by injury.

Mills was restricted to seven games, hurting his shoulder in a "Mad Monday" wrestling contest with a teammate before being ruled out of finals.

Cox's selection conundrum for Friday's clash is further complicated, with key forward Joel Amartey (Achilles) and winger Justin McInerney (hamstring) near full fitness.

Rampe said the Swans were playing the cards they were dealt.

"You've got one or two ways you can go in these circumstances," Rampe said.

"You can get the 'poor me' and feel sorry for yourself, or you can do something about it."

AAP

World.title: HYROX Beijing sparks backlash after Aussie athlete soils herself mid-race
World.content:
The organisers of a viral sporting event in Beijing have faced backlash and criticism after an Australian woman was allowed to continue competing after soiling herself.

Athlete Joanna Wietrzyk was participating in the global indoor fitness race HYROX in the Chinese capital at the weekend when she suffered a bout of faecal incontinence.

Wietrzyk was allowed to finish the course and won her event, with videos and photos posted online showing her continuing through demanding exercises and using communal equipment while visibly soiled.

The incident has gone viral on Chinese social media and sparked debate about HYROX's health and safety standards, as well as athlete responsibility.

"She's so selfish — she kept running the whole way even though she had diarrhoea," one user on Weibo questioned. "What about the runners behind her?"

Another wrote: "The host is ultimately unprofessional!"

On Weibo, the hashtag #Hyrox incontinence female competitor has not been punished# has more than 27 million views.

HYROX is a global fitness challenge in which participants race to complete often gruelling stations, including sandbag lunges, burpees, sled pushes and rowing.

An article on the Beijing incident was the most-viewed story on Chinese state media website the Global Times on Monday.

Joanna Wietrzyk (middle in black top) is an elite HYROX athlete who holds the Women's Solo Pro world record. (Instagram: joannawietrzyk)

In a statement, HYROX China said the area was decontaminated after the race had finished.

"After the incident, the organising committee immediately closed off and isolated the affected area and track, and completed comprehensive disinfection," organisers said.

"Relevant equipment was removed from the venue, and waste was disposed of in accordance with municipal waste-management standards."

The organisers also said they would replace flooring at the venue to protect future athlete health.

HYROX World also issued a statement addressing the incident.

"HYROX has clear bio-contaminant and medical procedures in place," the statement said.

"In this instance, an unforeseen situation arose in which protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were applied and understood."

The incident went viral on Chinese social media at the weekend and triggered strong backlash to the organisers. (Weibo, RedNote and Douyin)

But social media users and other athletes at the event have attacked the response and questioned why Wietrzyk was allowed to finish the race, potentially risking the health and safety of other competitors.

"For people who were exposed to that situation, there could be genuine physical and psychological consequences," one competitor named johopalooza posted on Instagram.

"I paid HYROX to provide a professionally organised and safe event. So while I understand the athlete perspective, ultimately my contract and expectation is with HYROX.

"Protecting athletes is important, but showing the wider community that HYROX takes responsibility when its own procedures fail is just as important."

Loading Instagram content

'Organisers should assess the risk'

HYROX has also been accused of double standards over its hygiene rules, which punish athletes with time penalties if they litter on the course, spit or clear their nose onto the floor.

HYROX has been contacted for comment.

Wietrzyk, who is a HYROX world record holder, was invited to compete at the Beijing event.

She has been contacted for comment.

Li Hongxin, an associate professor of sports management at China's Zhengzhou University of Light Industry, said the athlete should not be criticised or judged for experiencing a physiological problem.

"I think her determination and sportsmanship are very understandable," he said.

But he said the incident raised questions about the responsibility of event organisers.

"Organisers should assess whether such a situation could affect the health or wellbeing of other competitors," he said.

Dr Li said this was particularly important because HYROX was an indoor event.

"Take a marathon as an example. If a competitor is menstruating, organisers would generally respect their decision to continue because a marathon is an outdoor event," he said.

"They don't share equipment with other competitors, so it generally doesn't pose a public safety concern.

"But HYROX is an indoor event, where competitors share equipment. In that situation, I think the organisers should have staff step in and adjust the event, or take appropriate emergency measures."

World.title: Jordan Petaia returns to Wallabies squad after NFL stint
World.content:
Jordan Petaia has been selected in his first Wallabies squad since the 2023 Rugby World Cup as Les Kiss braces for the sternest test yet of his brief coaching reign.

A one-time teenage Test debutant, Petaia has been included in Australia's 34-man group for the upcoming showdown with back-to-back world champions South Africa in Perth.

The 26-year-old has been plying his trade in France and Japan since the end of the 2024 Super Rugby Pacific season, after seven seasons at the Queensland Reds.

He left the Reds in 2024 to pursue a career in the NFL, signing briefly for the Los Angeles Chargers in 2025, before being waived later that same year.

He then signed for Perpignan in the Top 14 before locking in a long-term spot at Urayasu D-Rocks.

Petaia made his Wallabies debut at just 19 at the 2019 World Cup in Japan, scoring a memorable try against Uruguay, and has since pulled on the gold jersey a total of 31 times.

With now just a year before Australia hosts the 2027 World Cup, Kiss says it's time to see if Petaia is ready to make a run at a third appearance at the global showpiece.

Jordan Petaia is set for a return to Wallaby gold. (Getty Images: PA Images/Bradley Collyer)

"Look, we've got a lot of good back-three players here in the country. We made sure we looked at all of them," Kiss said on Monday.

"It was just the ideal opportunity to see Jordan. He's been out of the system for a couple of years now. He has played in two World Cups. We just wanted to touch base with him, get him to come and work out with us, see how he's going.

"We haven't selected that team yet, but it was just a good opportunity to see Jordan back in the environment and him to have a good look at us with the new coaching structure and all those sort of things.

"From the team perspective, there was a lot of deep discussion about where we would go with that."

The classy utility back is one of three new faces in the squad that won back the Puma Trophy in an undefeated tour of Argentina earlier this month.

Another is Western Force recruit Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, who has been named in his first official Wallabies squad, replacing Carter Gordon who suffered a fractured calf bone in Mendoza.

Born in Toowoomba and raised in Gunnedah, the 22-year-old flyhalf was part of Australia's 2023 and 2024 World Rugby U20 Championships and has featured for the Reds on more than 35 occasions.

Queenslander Zane Nonggorr is back in the squad after completing a successful return to the field in Saturday's 2026 Super Rugby AUS opener having picked up a minor calf strain in Japan.

He replaces Wallaby number 1,000 Massimo De Lutiis, who is being managed after playing three straight Tests to kick off his international career.

Outside back Filipo Daugunu is also being managed due to a minor knee complaint.

"We've learned a bit more about ourselves as a group over the last four Tests and we know we still have a lot to work on to get to where we want to be," Kiss said of the Springboks challenge in Perth on September 27.

"South Africa have been the benchmark team in World Rugby for a long time and we're motivated by the challenge of meeting them in our own backyard in two weeks' time."

Wallabies Squad:

Forwards — Allan Alaalatoa, Angus Bell, Charlie Cale, Josh Canham, Tom Hooper, Isaac Kailea, Fraser McReight, Josh Nasser, Zane Nonggorr, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Billy Pollard, Aidan Ross, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Lachlan Shaw, Carlo Tizzano, Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Jeremy Williams, Harry Wilson (capt).

Backs: Jock Campbell, Ben Donaldson, Isaac Henry, Len Ikitau, Max Jorgensen, Ryan Lonergan, Tate McDermott, Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, Declan Meredith, Hunter Paisami, Jordan Petaia, Harry Potter, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Kalani Thomas, Tom Wright.

AAP

World.title: World Athletics firm on Russia ban, Coe acknowledges need for solution
World.content:
World Athletics president Sebastian Coe has said the governing body's position on the exclusion of Russian athletes has not changed ahead of an upcoming Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) case, while acknowledging the need for a resolution.

Russian Athletics last month filed a fresh appeal with CAS challenging sanctions imposed by World Athletics, which has barred Russian and Belarusian athletes from international competition since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Our position hasn't changed, and this isn't about politics or passports. It's about the integrity of competition," Coe told reporters on the final day of the inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest.

Aussie athletics star shocked at massive pay packet for coming second Australia's Nicola Olyslagers finishes second in the high jump at the new Ultimate Championship competition.

"From the age of 18, I believe that every position I've taken … it's about integrity and it's about competition, and that matters to me."

Coe declined to discuss the federation's legal strategy ahead of the arbitration proceedings but said World Athletics would continue to defend its stance.

"So our position won't change," he said. "And look, yes, this does need to be resolved, and I'm acutely aware of that. (But) I don't think our legal teams would be particularly thankful if I laid out our approach on this."

The comments came a month after Russian Athletics confirmed a new CAS filing, following an initial filing in July, aimed at overturning sanctions it says prevent it from fully representing Russian athletes internationally and participating in World Athletics decision-making processes.

Despite reaffirming the federation's position, Coe said he recognised the importance of ultimately restoring full global participation in the sport.

"We want a full complement of people on a global level competing in our sport, and that has to be our overall objective. Of course, it does."

The Lausanne-based CAS serves as sport's highest arbitration body and is expected to hear Russian Athletics' challenge in the coming months.

World Athletics has maintained one of the toughest positions of any international federation since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, while some sports have gradually reintroduced Russian and Belarusian athletes under neutral status.

The International Skating Union has established a pathway for selected Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete as neutral competitors, although it confirmed earlier this week that Kamila Valieva and three other figure skaters had their neutral status revoked.

Russian state news agency TASS quoted Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev as saying that all the skaters affected by the ruling would appeal to CAS.

Reuters

Tech.title: Is Big Tech’s AI slowdown a safety pact or a cartel?
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

When OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis, and SpaceX head Elon Musk loosely agreed over the weekend to slow down AI development, skeptics spotted an ulterior motive immediately. The AI titans had declared that their aim was to “pace the frontier,” signing on at least partially to a proposal for embedding third-party auditors, regulating domestic labs, and reaching a global slowdown agreement. Their critics, however, argued they simply wanted to stop would-be competitors, kneecap the open-source movement, and avoid real legal safeguards — some dubbed it an outright “cartel.”

The truth is more complicated, according to sources across the industry. The three-step proposal, laid out in an essay by Amodei, is calling for changes long espoused by AI safety advocates. While it could become a substitute for meaningful regulation, under Trump, regulation is unlikely anyway. But experts say that on an issue that’s only likely to grow in importance, AI leaders aren’t the best people to lead the charge.

“The industry as a whole needs new champions,” said Nick Reese, an adjunct professor at New York University and the Department of Homeland Security’s former director of emerging tech policy. “We’ve looked at people like Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk as these people who are closest to the problem and working on it every day, and they’re the ones who know best. But the truth is there’s never been a realistic vision for what we’re building toward.”

“The industry as a whole needs new champions.”

Concerns about AI have been escalating for months, sparked largely by revelations that agents were behind rogue hacks going on right under the noses of leading frontier labs Anthropic and OpenAI. Reports from both companies fueled the fire, as did the resignation of Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who posted a public letter explaining his choice. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he wrote, adding that neither OpenAI nor Anthropic is “acting responsibly” and rather “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

Dire warnings about AI aren’t anything new inside the industry, but Coxon’s letter seemed to break containment. It’s been viewed more than 170 million times on X alone, while Coxon and his story have made the rounds in newspapers and on TV.

To a significant chunk of AI safety researchers and AI nonprofit workers, however, this is simply drawing more attention to an already widely discussed issue. “A lot of people are thinking of this as Dario’s idea, or it’s coming from the CEOs, but that’s false,” said Daniel Kokotajlo, an ex-OpenAI employee who now leads the AI Futures Project, an AI research nonprofit. “People outside the companies have been calling for this for years … There’s been this growing chorus of voices saying, ‘Please don’t build superintelligence soon. We are not ready. You need to slow down.’”

Kokotajlo said that after years of people “yelling at them to do this” — including more than 1,000 AI lab employees signing a public letter from July, which called for a slowdown in AI development after the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident — the CEOs are now “now bowing to that pressure and also claiming credit for it, [although] not rightfully.”

Overall, a handful of sources told The Verge they believe that the verbal agreement made by the AI leaders is a step in the right direction. NYU’s Reese said he “do[es] not think it’s all hot air.” Apollo Research CEO Marius Hobbhahn called it “a good idea,” saying “it’s one of the best things for safety in a long time if it actually happens.” The Midas Project’s Tyler Johnston said it was a “good sign.” Redwood Research CEO Buck Shlegeris said it was “some great news — obviously it’s hard to know whether this is going to convert into anything real, but I’m feeling cautiously optimistic.” All agreed, though, that there was still a lot of work to do to make this verbal commitment a reality, particularly when it comes to making it an ironclad agreement.

“It’s one of the best things for safety in a long time if it actually happens.”

Many still question the motivations of AI’s leaders. The larger tech industry has spent years getting ahead of regulation by lobbying for its own preferred rules or promising self-regulation. Big platforms have proposed policies that could hit smaller competitors harder, using altruistic language to justify self-serving goals. They’ve been accused of safety-washing, or making meaningless changes that give the false impression of actual safeguards. It’s no surprise people are concerned this will happen in the AI industry as well, particularly since AI labs’ voluntary safety frameworks have been criticized for years.

Several sources believe that concerns of safety-washing are valid. “There’s a serious concern that they’re not actually going to slow down,” Kokotajlo says, adding that the fear is that “they’ll just bring in some external auditors, do a bunch of safety paperwork — some of which will be genuinely good — but at the end of the day, it actually won’t slow them down very much at all.”

NYU’s Reese compared this gambit to the social media platforms’ playbook a decade ago, when companies began calling for regulatory action to get ahead of impending, less favorable laws. For the AI industry, Reese said, “the hammer may not come in this administration, but I think if there were a Democratic administration after the next election, there would be a really good possibility.”

That kind of regulation would be vital, said Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project — any voluntary framework is essentially regulatory capture and that “we should not be letting the foxes run the henhouse. This is not an opportunity for Congress to once again outsource responsibility to industry.” Daniel Lobo-Lewis, co-founder of the Political Integrity Project, said that voluntary regulation will likely go the way of Meta’s largely toothless Oversight Board.

Most people also, however, believe companies are in no imminent danger. President Trump posted on Monday that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” He also called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while Huang was onstage at a conference — Trump told the crowd on speakerphone that recent concerns about AI were a “hoax” and that “the robots will not be taking over.”

As for concerns that regulation could hold back other companies or open source developers, calls for slowdowns have been almost exclusively aimed at big frontier AI labs defined by exact size metrics, many industry experts told The Verge.

With no government AI regulation incoming, the best option may be to push companies into an immediate, measurable, and enforceable agreement. Kokotajlo’s AI Futures Project, for instance, proposed AI labs giving auditors access to their compute budget. Amodei’s essay already called for AI labs to allow external third-party auditors — like METR, Apollo, and Redwood Research — to embed within their organizations to some extent and potentially be able to flag, and blow the whistle on, problematic findings. Kokotajlo says companies would ideally need to cut down their own compute budgets for research in the process, slowing down development and allowing other AI labs to catch up.

“If I am going to die at the hands of killer AI, I want it to be American, not Chinese.”

Arguably the single biggest challenge to an AI slowdown can be summarized in one word: China.

AI leaders and politicians alike have long positioned China as the reason why US AI progress can’t slow down — because no matter how dangerous the technology may become, they’d rather it be in US hands than Chinese ones, and China won’t pump the brakes. Lobo-Lewis compared China fears to the Cold War missile gap. One X user wrote, “If I am going to die at the hands of killer AI, I want it to be American, not Chinese.”

Redwood Research’s Shlegeris said it wasn’t in the best interest of neither the US nor the Chinese government to pursue AI development in a “reckless” way, adding that “it would not be unprecedented levels of international coordination.”
